title: The governance of snarking: Anti-fandom as tiny publics
abstract: This article examines online celebrity ‘snarking’ communities, otherwise known as anti-fandom spaces or even hate forums. Specifically, we provide an analysis of the governance of these groups and how they develop a collective morality through both articulations with the celebrities’ mediation and with the logics of social justice. Using data collected from a digital ethnography of two popular celebrity snark spaces, we employ Critical Discourse Analysis to track the particular discursive repertoires and vernaculars which characterise snark across multiple platforms. We argue that despite the perceived ‘incivility’ of these online spaces, discourses of care, justice and solidarity often emerge which complicate existing narratives of these groups. Though participation in snarking collectives is often explained in pathologising or individualising narratives of anti-fandom, we demonstrate some of the reflexive work that happens in these spaces which sometimes ignites sociological discussions and frustrations at inequalities. We therefore conceptualise snark through the lens of a ‘tiny public’ that identifies and explores broader race and class injustice in contemporary society. Here, the prevailing discourses about celebrity subjects ‘failing upwards’ betrays an anger at elites who do not suffer the same material consequences at times of crisis; though many of these frustrations are misdirected back at the celebrity subject and manifest in a collective desire to see repercussions for the individual celebrity, rather than collective action aimed at the structures that make this failure possible, visible and even lucrative.

title: Exorbitant Privilege of the Periodic Table? Geoeconomics, Endogenous Centrality and Strategic Minerals for the Green Transition,
authors: Josh Kirk, Evgenia Passari, Hélène Rey
abstract: Trade networks underpinning the energy transition are endogenous economic objects, and their structure is a source of market power. Using bilateral trade data for thirteen electrification metals over 1995–2023, we show that trade in these materials has reorganised into a hub-and-spoke system centred on China, in sharp contrast to the more diffuse, multilateral structure of fossil fuels. This centrality did not follow from resource endowments: China holds few of the underlying reserves. It was built through processing investment, industrial policy, and commodity-targeted development finance, an equilibrium outcome rather than a geographical accident. We formalise this logic in a stylised model in which a country chooses how central to become, and show that centrality can map into pricing power: the response of the world price of critical minerals to a supply cut is stronger when the network is more concentrated, the downstream demand and the competitive fringe supply are more inelastic. Constructing text-based, commodity-specific supply shocks and estimating local projections, we find that supply contractions in critical metals raise consumer inflation in the European Union and the United States by roughly twice as much as comparable fossil-fuel shocks, and more persistently. Centrality is therefore not merely a descriptive feature of the new resource map: it can create leverage over global prices. The green transition reduces strategic dependence on hydrocarbon exporters but reconstitutes it around the architecture of mineral supply chains.

title: Drought: Impacts, Prevention, and Adaptation Options Across Scales
authors: Ermias Aynekulu, Gudeta W. Sileshi, Charles N. Wamucii, Mohamed Imam Bakarr, Ulrich Apel, Guadalupe Duron, Daniel Tsegai, Meine van Noordwijk
abstract: Beyond lack of water, drought means that expected levels of water availability are not realized, triggering cascading consequences across land, water, biodiversity, climate, and human systems. Drought reflects variation in water availability, including thresholds, frequency, intensity, duration, and spatial synchrony as well as how expectations and anticipation shape human actions. Drought symptoms are linked to local pressures and broader drivers of change and can induce social and ecological responses. This review synthesizes advances in understanding the biophysical and socioeconomic impacts of drought across temporal scales, from seasonal to multi-year and climatic drought, and across subsystem typologies, including meteorological, hydrological, agricultural, ecological, and socioeconomic drought. The review demonstrates how weakened ecological buffers, governance failures, and policy incoherence intensify drought vulnerability. Building drought resilience requires coordinated action across sectors, scales, and institutions to restore the ecological, social, and governance buffers that sustain human well-being and planetary stability. title: Regime Shifts and Transformations in Social-Ecological Systems: Advancing Critical Frontiers for Safe and Just Futures
authors: Juan C. Rocha, Caroline Schill, Emilie A.L. Lindkvist, Reinette Biggs, Thorsten Blenckner, Anne-Sophie Crépin, Ingo Fetzer, Carl Folke, Amanda Jiménez-Aceituno, Nielja Knecht, Jan J. Kuiper, Steven J. Lade, Carla Lanyon-Garrido, Romi Lotcheris, Romina Martin, Vanessa Masterson, Petr Matous, Michele-Lee Moore, Magnus Nyström, Per Olsson, Laura M. Pereira, Garry Peterson, André Pinto da Silva, Sasha Quahe, Maja Schlüter, Uno Svedin, Lan Wang-Erlandsson, Hannah Zoller
abstract: Current research challenges in sustainability science require us to consider nonlinear changes—shifts that do not happen gradually but can be sudden and difficult to predict. Central questions are therefore how we can prevent harmful shifts, promote desirable ones, and better anticipate both. The regime shifts and transformations literature is well-equipped to address these questions. Yet, even though both research streams stem from the same intellectual roots, they have developed along different paths, with limited exchange between the two, missing opportunities for cross-fertilization. We here review the definitions and history of both research streams to disentangle common grounds and differences. We propose avenues for future research and highlight how stronger integration of both research streams could support the development of more powerful approaches to help us navigate toward safe and just futures.

title: In Pursuit of Spatial, Life‐Course and Social Mobilities: Aspiring Filipino Seafarers Acquiring Migration Ability Through Servitude
abstract: This article examines aspiring Filipino seafarers' pursuit of the triple mobilities : spatial (migration), life course (education to work, youth to adulthood) and social. It focuses on those working as ‘utility cadets’ for manning agencies that supply seafarers to ship operators in exchange for a ship placement. Its aims are twofold. Based on long‐term research and drawing on interviews with utility cadets, successful seafarers who were once utility cadets, and parents or older siblings of utility cadets, it first conceptualises as ability acquisition how aspiring Filipino seafarers turn servitude into a strategy to accumulate the ability to migrate. Second, it shows how this spatial mobility enables their life‐course and social mobilities, and accounts for how these three mobilities are interconnected. The pace of life‐course mobility shaped and was shaped by the degree of the seafarers' contribution to their family's social mobility , and both constituted and were constituted by the seafarers' rank in the seafaring labour hierarchy, which determined their salary. The article further conceptualises the intertwinement of the triple mobilities by explaining their negotiation through processes of convergence and divergence .

title: Reconceptualising Social Integration: Experiences of Internal Youth Migrants in Ghana
authors: Francis Diawuo Darko, Susanne Schech, Udoy Saikia
abstract: Research on migrant social integration has focused mainly on international migration, leaving internal migration, especially in the Global South, underexplored as a site of theory‑building. This paper reconceptualises social integration through an empirical study of young internal migrants in Sunyani, Ghana, a secondary city characterised by informality and decentralised governance. Drawing on a mixed‑methods design of survey data and qualitative narrative interviews, the analysis shows that integration is not a linear or place‑bound outcome but a negotiated process shaped by material precarity, social relations, institutional mediation, and sustained connections to places of origin. While economic participation and co‑ethnic bonding networks enable survival in the informal economy, limited cross‑group trust and exclusionary encounters with local authorities constrain broader inclusion. Importantly, the paper advances translocality as a constitutive dimension of social integration, showing that ongoing obligations to origin communities function as adaptive strategies for managing risk and belonging in contexts of weak urban safety nets, while simultaneously reshaping local embedding. By foregrounding internal migration in a secondary African city, the study challenges state‑centred and settlement‑based integration models and contributes to population geography by reframing social integration as a spatially distributed, relational process within national borders.

title: Deceptive Citizenship as an Instrument of New War: Authoritarian Practices in a Post‐Colonial Context
abstract: The article demonstrates how, under authoritarian practices and post‐colonialism, a state employs deceptive citizenship as an instrument of a ‘new war.’ The deceptive citizenship operates within informational autocracy for a selected category of migrantised people, which make them unaware about the legal, political and mobility consequences of this status. By obscuring the legal, political, and mobility consequences of this status, it enables authorities to symbolically project power beyond territorial boundaries and consolidate their geopolitical post‐colonial standing among citizens. Using Russia's citizenship policies towards displaced Ukrainians between 2014 and 2022 as a case study, this article traces the complex genealogy of these policies and shows how, prior to the full‐scale invasion, they served geopolitical ambitions and postcolonial hegemony. At the same time, it demonstrates that displaced Ukrainians' citizenship practices were driven primarily by the need to cope with uncertainty and insecurity.

title: Neighbourhood Ethnic Diversification in Urban and Rural England and Wales
authors: Richard Wright, Gemma Catney, Mark Ellis, Momoko Nishikido
abstract: The minority ethnic share of the population of England and Wales rose from 8.7% in 2001 to over 18% in 2021. Using 2001, 2011 and 2021 Census data for England and Wales with consistent neighbourhood boundaries, this paper investigates how these aggregate changes translated into alterations in neighbourhood ethnic composition across the urban–rural continuum. We classify neighbourhoods into three diversity types (low, moderate, high) via an entropy‑based metric and track transitions over two decades. Ethnic and racial diversity grew in all neighbourhood types and geographic settings. Between 2001 and 2021, neighbourhoods with all‐White populations all but disappeared, neighbourhoods classified as low diversity with a large White majority declined in number, and counts of moderately diverse neighbourhoods increased. Additionally, the proportion of highly diverse (multiethnic) neighbourhoods tripled during this period. These changes follow a broadly hierarchical pattern, focused first, and most intensively, in London and subsequently occurring in secondary Metropolitan counties and relatively smaller urban settings. Finally, we detect some decade‐specific differences, notably a deceleration in neighbourhood transitions toward greater ethnic diversity between 2011 and 2021. A counterfactual analysis of the consolidation of ethnic diversity into moderately diverse neighbourhoods rather than further condensation into high diversity spaces suggests the rising importance of locational preferences and constraints relative to demographic forces in shaping these new neighbourhood geographies.

title: The Factors Driving Migration Intentions and Destination Preferences in Central, East, and Southeast European Countries
authors: Antea Barišić, Mahdi Ghodsi, Alireza Sabouniha, Robert Stehrer
abstract: This paper studies the determinants of the intentions to emigrate and conditional on migration aspirations, the destination choice in a number of Central East and Southeast European economies (CESEE). Using data from the OeNB Euro Survey, we apply a two‐stage Heckman procedure to identify the drivers of migration intentions – specifically individuals' demographic and household attributes, financial conditions, past economic experiences, and future expectations. In the second stage, conditional on the stated intention to migrate, we examine the determinants of destination choice, distinguishing between EU15, EU‐CEE, and extra‐EU countries. This micro‐level evidence indicates that economic and financial conditions (past, present, and expected) play an important role in shaping migration intentions, while non‐economic factors, including individual demographic and family attributes, as well as network ties, also exert important influence. Destination preferences, conditional on an already existing intention to migrate are not simply a mechanical extension of intention determinants. The choice of the destination region is determined mostly by marital status, educational attainment, and GDP per capita variables in the origin and destination region. This reflects the conceptualisation of migration as a two‐stage decision process, distinguishing between entry into the pool of potential migrants and destination choice within that pool. This stage‐specific perspective thus allows to differentiate determinants of intentions and destination choice of prospective mobility, that empirical results based on actual migration decisions cannot deliver.

title: Household Assets and Internal Mobility in Laos: Agricultural Land, Home Ownership, and Multi‐Stream Population Redistribution
abstract: Internal migration in agrarian economies is usually framed as a rural‐to‐urban transition, but population redistribution follows multiple pathways. Household assets such as land and housing shape these moves, and how they do so is contested: some research finds that assets anchor households in place, while other work finds that they enable movement. This debate has centred on rural‐to‐urban flows in settings of uneven ownership, leaving open how assets relate to the full range of mobility, including non‐migration and rural‐bound moves, where ownership is near‐universal. This study examines that question in Lao PDR, a setting of gradual urbanisation and continued rural dominance. Drawing on the nationally representative Lao Social Indicator Survey, it models three outcomes: migration versus non‐migration, rural versus urban residence among non‐migrants, and the direction of movement among migrants. Two findings emerge. First, mobility in Laos is multidirectional rather than a single rural‐to‐urban flow: measured against rural–urban migration, rural–rural movement is about three times as common, and urban–urban and urban–rural flows each about twice as common. Second, ownership and renting point in opposite directions: agricultural land and home ownership accompany staying and rural‐bound movement, while renting and internet access accompany urban‐oriented mobility. Notably, urban residence does not preclude landholding: most urban residents still own farmland. These findings extend the population geography of assets and mobility beyond the rural‐to‐urban paradigm, revealing a household‐level dual attachment in which the same assets anchor and enable mobility at once.

title: Why Comply? Explaining Sectoral Patterns in GRECO 'S Anti‐Corruption Recommendations
abstract: Why do states vary in their compliance with international anti‐corruption recommendations? Research often treats the state as a unitary actor and explains variation at country‐level. This article challenges that assumption by examining variation in compliance across institutional sectors within countries. Using original data from the Council of Europe's Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), the analysis shows a clear sectoral pattern. Recommendations addressed to prosecutors are implemented most frequently, followed by those targeting judges, while recommendations directed at members of parliament show the lowest levels of compliance. The article explains this variation through the political economy of target compliance. Reform outcomes depend on the interaction between the political costs imposed by reform and the degree of control that targeted actors exercise over its implementation. We find little evidence that country‐level factors shape reform outcomes, while sector‐specific incentives provide a stronger explanation for compliance patterns. By highlighting the importance of the target population, the article contributes to research on international compliance, anti‐corruption governance, and international monitoring mechanisms.

title: A Rapid Systematic Map of Youth Engagement With Marine Environments in a Changing Climate
authors: Carlo Ceglia, Alexandra C. Morel, Lorraine van Blerk
abstract: This paper offers a rapid systematic map of existing qualitative literature on the relationship(s) between marine environments and youth in a changing climate. Building upon recent public, scientific, and scholarly trends that draw attention to the value the ocean holds for both socio‐economic prosperity and climate regulation, this systematic map asks: What evidence emerges from qualitative studies of youth engagement with marine environments in a changing climate? The mapping identified 20 articles thematically coded under three categories—namely, (i) youth experiences of marine environments and climate change, (ii) marine‐based pedagogical approaches to climate change, and (iii) creative strategies and new media. Along with these 3 main categories, the mapping identified different cross‐cutting themes that the 20 studies share. These were discussed as (a) the importance of intergenerational dynamics and intergenerational justice, (b) the lack of youth's insights in marine‐based climate discourses, and (c) the need for place‐based socio‐cultural and economic interventions. After presenting and discussing the results, this rapid systematic map concludes by indicating areas for further research. Specifically, it highlights the need for more place‐based, granular approaches that engage young people on their own terms and experiences as having tremendous value for articulating more ocean‐ and climate‐sensitive interventions. At the same time, it cautions that those same interventions must feed into wider socio‐economic and institutional dynamics that account for the historical responsibilities of a changing climate.

How Recipients Compose Their News Sources Online: Utilizing Tracking Data to Investigate Digital News Media Repertoires
authors: Robin Leuppert, Jule Scheper, Nico Spreen, Elena Link
abstract: Today’s high-choice media environment offers various opportunities for interest-driven news exposure, resulting in highly diverse and fragmented news usage patterns, especially in the digital media environment. Media repertoires provide a suitable theoretical framework for considering these circumstances and investigating the entirety and interrelatedness of individuals’ news sources, rather than focusing on singular news offerings. We explore media repertoires focusing on news by relying on behavioral tracking data from 805 German respondents over eleven weeks (November 2022–January 2023). Conducting a latent class analysis based on news usage frequencies across seventeen news categories, we identified eight digital news media repertoires with distinct usage patterns. Repertoire comparisons via analysis of variance (ANOVA) further revealed differences in the news topics used, users’ diversity of news outlets, news concentration, and news usage duration. Implications for future research on investigating media repertoire compositions are discussed.

title: The Policy Umwelt: How AI Problem Representations Render Governance Alternatives Unthinkable
abstract: This paper investigates how AI narratives actively constrain the horizon of conceivable governance options. Moving beyond the established finding that narratives influence policy, we argue they fundamentally prefigure the scope of the politically thinkable by creating what we term “Policy Umwelten.” Adapting Jakob von Uexküll’s concept, a Policy Umwelt describes the perceptible and actionable landscape of interventions available within a given narrative, which systematically renders alternatives invisible. We analyze three competing narratives: Existential Risk, Accelerationism, and Critical AI. We do so through a “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” analysis of their foundational manifestos. Each constructs a distinct Umwelt: Existential Risk makes global technocratic containment imperative; Accelerationism legitimizes only deregulation and market liberation; and Critical AI centers structural reform. Despite their overt conflict, these narratives converge in constructing Policy Umwelten that render a pragmatic approach to governance difficult to perceive: one that emphasizes iterative learning from empirical feedback and institutional flexibility over grand visions or predetermined certainties. The paper concludes that the most significant constraint on AI policy is not a lack of options but a collective failure of political perception. The Policy Umwelt concept thus provides a diagnostic tool for mapping ideological deadlock and identifying pathways toward more adaptive and less deterministic technological futures.

title: Whose Digital Future? Civil Society and Alternative Imaginaries in Transnational Digital Governance
abstract: This article investigates different visions of digital futures, examining how desired futures are discursively constructed within civil society in transnational digital governance. The analysis builds on discourse theory and a growing body of research on imaginaries in digital governance. Through a discourse‐theoretical analysis of submission papers to the United Nations' Global Digital Compact, the article examines how different collective actors within civil society construct and mobilise desired futures in the institutional context of the UN. The study finds discursive elements that articulate three distinct digital futures: technological progress, societal balance and transformative change. While their objectives, obstacles and enablers are constructed in diverse ways, in all three, digital technologies are considered necessary. By illuminating different normative values and the affective potential through which individuals and collectives are positioned in relation to desired futures, these findings show a variety of articulations within civil society and offer insights into its normative and political roles. In doing so, this study contributes to an understanding of the possibilities and limitations of alternatives in digital governance.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on heat thresholds for maternal health and birth outcomes
authors: Clara S. Heil, Leonidas G. Ioannou, Günter Alce, Susanne Frennert, Chuansi Gao
abstract: Global warming poses major public health challenges, with pregnant individuals particularly vulnerable to heat. We aim to synthesise evidence on the effects of ambient heat on pregnancy and birth outcomes and identify heat thresholds associated with increased risk of these adverse outcomes. We searched Medline, Web of Science, Scopus, GreenFile and Cinahl (June 2024) for peer-reviewed studies reporting thresholds for ambient heat; heat from medical devices, saunas, pools or studies on conception, IVF, postnatal health were excluded. Participants within studies are limited to individuals capable of becoming pregnant, including women and those identifying differently. Risk of bias is assessed using the Office of Health Assessment and Translation tool. Findings are narratively synthesised according to outcome and exposure metric, and a random effects meta-regression is used to estimate heat thresholds for acute heat effects on adverse outcomes. Evidence is limited by heterogeneity and methodological variability among studies included, and through review process limitations, including no independent dual data extraction and single person performing quality assessment. Meta-analyses determine Tmax thresholds 30.55 °C, 34.11 °C and 39.07 °C for 5%, 10% and 20% risk increase (21 studies, sample=5,589,862), suggesting increasing risk of adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes with increasing heat. The narrative syntheses (103 studies, sample=41,951,950) identifies heterogeneous indicators and a lack of comprehensive heat stress indices. Funding was received through the European Union’s Horizon Framework Programme and UKRI Innovate. PROSPERO registration: CRD42024610438.

title: Tracking funding disparities in global health aid with machine learning
authors: Finn Stürenburg, Kerstin Forster, Nicolas Banholzer, Malte Toetzke, Kenneth Harttgen, Stefan Feuerriegel
abstract: Reducing the global burden of disease is crucial for improving health outcomes. However, misalignment between health aid and country-level disease burden leaves vulnerable populations without the necessary support for major health challenges, particularly in the least developed countries. Here, we develop a machine learning pipeline using large language models to track flows in official development assistance (ODA) earmarked for health and identify aid–burden misalignment. We classified 3.7 million development aid projects from 2000 to 2022 (USD ~ 332 billion) into 17 major categories of communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional diseases (CMNNDs) and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). We compared the rank of per capita ODA disbursement against the rank of disease burden, measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). We interpret DALY-based alignment as a policy-relevant heuristic rather than a prescriptive allocation criterion. Although funding and disease burden are significantly correlated for many diseases, there are notable disparities. For example, NCDs account for 59.5% of global DALYs but received only 2.5% of health-related ODA over the study period. This is concerning because low- and middle-income countries face an increasing double burden from both CMNNDs and NCDs. Our results show aid–burden misalignment across multiple diseases in several regions, including Central Africa and parts of South Asia and West Africa. Overall, our results identify health disparities to potentially inform policy decisions on development assistance and support targeted allocation of health aid.

title: The Tangrams Codeswitching Corpus
authors: Anne L. Beatty-Martínez, Jiaze Li, Yumeng Shen, Stanislav Mulík, Robert D. Hawkins, Rosa E. Guzzardo Tamargo, Paola E. Dussias
abstract: Most research in the language sciences has centered on monolingual data, limiting the relevance of its insights for multilingual populations. The Tangrams Codeswitching Corpus , a Spanish-English dataset containing 30,858 words from 45 dyadic repeated reference games, bridges this gap by offering a richly annotated dataset on bilingual communication and codeswitching. In addition to the corpus, the dataset includes detailed metadata on language experience and proficiency of 90 habitual codeswitchers, enabling studies of individual differences in social coordination and switching behavior. This publicly available resource is valuable for exploring bilinguals’ language choices and the interactional dynamics through which they communicate, collaborate, and coordinate with one another. By providing a transdisciplinary perspective on codeswitching, this dataset offers a unique opportunity to explore how bilinguals adapt their language choices and communicative behavior in everyday interaction.

title: From Fringe to Power in the TikTok Age: Libertarian Ideology and Transgressive Performances in Milei’s ‘Populism Without the People’
authors: Ana Ines Langer, Lluis de Nadal, Eugenia Mitchelstein
abstract: Democracies around the world are under strain from radical right populist leaders and parties, raising urgent questions about their appeal. One way to approach this is by examining what and how they communicate on social media. TikTok warrants close attention, not only as the fastest-growing platform for news and information, but also because of the wider ‘Tiktokification’ of social media and the growing importance of visual communication. Yet populist communication on TikTok has received little attention, reflecting a broader text-centric bias in the literature. Here, we trace Javier Milei’s journey from the political margins to the Argentine presidency through his communication on TikTok, a platform considered key to his electoral success. We combine content analysis of text, visual and performative dimensions and show that Milei rarely appeals to ‘the people’—striking given ‘people-centrism’ is typically considered populism’s defining feature. This is, however, consistent with his right-wing libertarian ideology, which elevates individual freedom over collective solidarity, and is fitting with TikTok’s individualised mode of consumption. Milei’s populism without ‘the people,’ as we call it, combines contempt for the State, anti-elitism and transgressive performances that, as our regression analysis reveals, generate higher engagement. These findings advance our understanding of populism beyond the Global North and for a leader celebrated by the populist radical right worldwide, with broader implications for the relationship between populism, digital media and liberal democracy.

Who belongs to the demos? Undemocratic penalties to immigrant minority representation
authors: Beyza E. Buyuker, Alexandra Filindra, Mia K. Gandenberger, Eva T. Green, Anita Manatschal
abstract: Opposition to political candidates who represent ethnic minority interests in Western societies has included calls for undemocratic penalties. Majority groups in democratic societies value democracy in principle, but such support is malleable. We argue that diverse societies lack consensus on who constitutes the “demos”, the imagined political community. When there is a mismatch between a citizen’s understanding of the demos and an officeholder’s background and/or agenda, citizens may be open to imposing undemocratic penalties by reclassifying the offender as a demos-outsider and/or the punishing action as democratic. We tested our expectations with three survey experiments in the US and Switzerland that varied the candidate’s background (majority v. immigrant minority) and agenda (advocating for an age quota v. ethnic diversity quota). Results confirm that citizens do not behave as principled democrats but rather use their understanding of the demos to support or reject undemocratic penalties against minority politicians and policies. Their vision of the demos also determines whether they perceive the candidate as a demos-outsider (not “true” American/Swiss) and his banning as democratic. Interestingly, support for undemocratic penalties is on average higher in Switzerland than in the US, and slight nuances in the empirical results point to certain contextual contingencies of our results. Overall, our cross-country results suggest that people’s understanding of democracy is not based on firm institutional and procedural criteria, but on distinct visions about who belongs, and who does not.

title: Uneven patterns of cross-border media coverage following natural disasters
abstract: Many natural disasters central to climate-policy debates are hydro-meteorological hazards, yet it remains unclear how media attention is distributed across disaster types. Using 135 million news articles from 466 sources in 123 countries since 2016, we estimated cross-border reporting changes after disasters. Attention rises but is highly uneven (95% confidence intervals are shown in parentheses after the estimates): short-run increases are largest following earthquakes ( β = 0.0785 (0.0758, 0.0812)), dry-mass movements ( β = 0.0531 (0.0349, 0.0713)) and volcanic eruptions ( β = 0.0425 (0.0359, 0.0490)), and smaller for floods ( β = 0.0069 (0.0062, 0.0076)) and droughts ( β = 0.0001 (−0.0036, 0.0039)). Conditional on severity and duration, hydro-meteorological disasters receive less attention than geophysical disasters ( θ = −0.0065 (−0.0115, −0.0015)). Coverage is higher for 100+ versus 0–9 deaths ( β = 0.0360 (0.0231, 0.0490)), with stronger fatality gradients for country pairs with tighter social ties ( β = 0.1498 (0.0822, 0.2174)) and ancestral relatedness ( β = 0.2965 (0.1887, 0.4043)).

authors: Lucas Straub, Philipp Trotter, Elsie Onsongo, Detlef van Vuuren, Julian Kirchherr
abstract: The circular economy (CE) is widely viewed as a key global lever for sustainable resource use. However, CE conceptualizations have focused mostly on high resource use in the Global North, largely neglecting the drivers, solutions and enablers of circularity in the socio-economic contexts of the Global South. Here, based on a systematic review of 183 peer-reviewed articles, we assess how CE manifests in the Global South. We find circular solutions to be considerably more bottom-up, centring around community-level and often informal practices rather than the top-down, policy and industrially driven activities that dominate the Global North-informed CE literature. CE motivations similarly differ, being primarily rooted in socio-economic needs and cultural practices rather than environmental concerns. Finally, CE enablers are often based on socially and technically adaptive approaches rather than technological innovation. These differences reveal that inclusive circular pathways for sustainable development depend strongly on context, suggesting the need for more flexible and empirically grounded CE concepts.

authors: Svetlana Khromova, Svea Busse, Giulia Benati, Pablo Herreros-Cantis, Charlie Mioulet, Matthew J Eckelman, Gara Villalba-Méndez, Johannes Langemeyer

title: Population dispersion around cities as a driver of global urban land expansion
authors: Francesco Orsi, Diego Valbuena, Alvaro Hopkins
abstract: Urbanization implies a massive expansion of built-up land globally. The magnitude of this phenomenon, however, largely depends on the degree to which growing urban populations spatially concentrate around existing settlements. Here we measure population centrality, or the inverse of residents’ average travel time to the urban core, in over 7000 urban areas worldwide between 2000 and 2020, and test its association with urban land expansion. We observe rising dispersion (i.e., lower centrality) in most urban areas everywhere except Europe and the Americas. This is concerning as the two variables are negatively related: all else being equal, each additional minute from the urban core comes with an extra 1.6 km 2 of built-up land. The association, however, is clearly negative only in small- to mid-sized and low- to mid-income urban areas, but poorly so otherwise. Moreover, higher centrality goes hand-in-hand with a modest containment of built-up land in Southeast Asia, Europe, Canada, and the USA, and an expansion of it in Eastern Asia and Oceania. Our findings suggest that increasing centrality may be a powerful tool for curbing urban land expansion in certain contexts, but an ineffective one in others, and that planning is needed to mitigate the spillovers of centralization.

title: Nature contact can level up income inequities in mental health: evidence for equigenesis in Australia
authors: Thomas Astell-Burt, Tanya Pritchard, Brenda Lin, Richard Mitchell, Xiaoqi Feng

title: Nature-based solutions for whom - Europeanization and co-optation of collaborative NBS in authoritarian Belgrade
abstract: This paper explores how Nature-Based Solutions (NBS), introduced through processes of Europeanization, are grounded in, and co-opted by, the post-socialist, neoliberal, and increasingly authoritarian Belgrade. The analysis focuses on the EU-funded CLEVER Cities project, which introduced NBS to Belgrade through the Linear Park, which was later absorbed into Marina Dorćol—a commercial waterfront development by European investors. Despite being celebrated as a best - practice example, the paper indicates that the NBS framework built on participation and socio-ecological benefits is turned into a tool for profit-making and political legitimation by an increasingly authoritarian Serbian regime. Building on document and media analysis, the paper identifies how this local co-optation of NBS is both mediated and reinforced by processes of Europeanization. The findings contribute to the critical debates on NBS by revealing structural limitations rooted not only in the local context but also in the way NBS are created and diffused in Europe. The paper argues for more politically reflexive approaches to NBS that prioritize power redistribution and social justice across diverse urban contexts.

title: Conversation Without Conversion: Evidence from Cross-Partisan Interactions on a Mobile Chat Platform
abstract: Recent research on political persuasion suggests that narrative- and evidence-based messages can effectively change attitudes in settings such as canvassing, video presentations, and survey experiments. Yet less is known about how these persuasive strategies operate in two-way, cross-partisan political conversations. This study examines the relationship between persuasive message types, conversational reciprocity, and post-discussion attitudes using survey and text data from 966 U.S. participants engaged in anonymous one-on-one political discussions on DiscussIt, a mobile chat platform. I analyze how evidence-based arguments and personal narratives relate to both conversational interaction outcomes and measurable attitude change. Participants exposed to more personal narratives were more likely to perceive their conversation partner as influential and reported more positive conversational experiences, particularly when narrative exchanges were mutually reciprocated. In contrast, evidence-based exchanges were associated with lower perceived interpersonal influence, lower conversational enjoyment, and greater perceptions of relative knowledge. Despite these differences in conversational dynamics, neither persuasive strategy nor conversation structure was associated with significant changes in immediate or delayed political attitudes. Unlike studies of one-way persuasive messages, this research examines spontaneous peer-to-peer political conversations. Results suggest that persuasive strategies influence relational and experiential outcomes more than political attitudes.

title: Body image and food content on TikTok: exploring the influence of TikTok videos on users’ body image
abstract: The emergence of new media and its effects on users’ communication and behavior have been of interest to scholars. The study aims to add to the literature by analyzing the TikTok platform and the influence of TikTok's ‘What I eat in a day’ videos on body image. The research will draw on social comparison theory and utilize experiment as a method. The analysis extends the theoretical and methodological framework of videos about food on online platforms through the lens of TikTok.

title: From content immunity to design accountability: youth social media addiction litigation after the Meta and YouTube negligence verdict
abstract: This paper examines how recent youth social media addiction litigation, centered on the 2026 Meta and YouTube verdict, reframes harm as a problem of negligent design rather than third-party content. Using doctrinal legal analysis and policy synthesis, it argues that addictive-design and failure-to-warn claims may narrow Section 230’s practical reach, reshape understandings of duty and foreseeability, and support safety-by-design regulation. The paper positions youth litigation as a site for rethinking platform accountability in communication law.

title: Implementing a State-Owned Utility's Promotional Discount Program: A Case Study of PLN's “Diskon Tambah Daya 50%” Initiative and Its Contribution to Customer Uptake and Business Sustainability
abstract: This report presents a case study of the implementation of PT PLN (Persero) Unit Induk Distribusi Jawa Barat's “Diskon Tambah Daya 50%” (50% Additional Power Discount) program, a time-bound promotional initiative offering a 50% reduction in connection fees (Biaya Penyambungan, BP) to residential and business customers seeking to increase their electrical capacity. Conducted during the author's internship placement in the Commerce and Customer Management (Niaga dan Manajemen Pelanggan) division, this study documents the program's design, promotional execution, and operational realization, and situates the initiative within the broader context of customer-oriented marketing strategy and public-sector business sustainability practice. Data were gathered through direct participation, field observation, structured interviews with the internship supervisor, and review of internal program documentation. The author's principal contribution was the development of promotional media as part of the program's customer-acquisition strategy. As of 27 July 2026, program realization data show that 12,273 of a targeted 14,164 customers (86.65%) had completed payment, of whom 10,231 (83.36%) had been technically activated, generating Rp6.99 billion in connection-fee revenue and 14.63 MVA of additional contracted capacity. Six of the unit's service areas (Depok, Bandung, Cimahi, Bekasi, Sumedang, and Gunung Putri) exceeded their assigned targets. The findings illustrate how coordinated cross-unit implementation, multi- channel promotional communication, and time-bound pricing incentives can jointly support both short-term revenue objectives and longer-term customer base expansion for a state-owned utility. The report concludes with practical reflections on program execution and recommendations for strengthening future thematic promotional initiatives within PLN's customer management function. Keywords: promotional pricing, connection-fee discount, customer acquisition, state-owned enterprise, business sustainability, PT PLN (Persero)

title: You Have My Attention: Offline Events and the Temporal Dynamics of Online Harassment in Politics
abstract: The online harassment of politicians has become a defining feature of contemporary digital politics. While existing research has documented the forms and consequences of online harassment, less attention has been paid to how salient offline events shape its temporal dynamics. This study examines the relationship between salient offline events, such as wildfires and political resignations, and online harassment directed at Canadian federal Members of Parliament (MPs) on YouTube throughout 2024. We find that while a baseline level of harassment is consistently present, salient offline events are associated with short-term fluctuations in harassment, with comments increasing in the few days following an event. However, enduring structural factors, particularly MPs' gender and political party affiliation, are stronger predictors of harassment than offline events. By foregrounding time as an analytical dimension, this research advances our understanding of how offline events shape the temporal dynamics of online harassment while highlighting the structural factors that sustain it.

title: Is the Justice Cascade Over? Accountability in an Era of Impunity
authors: Averell Schmidt, Kathryn Sikkink, Geoff Dancy
abstract: The emergence of individual criminal accountability for war crimes, mass atrocities, and the violation of human rights is among the most dramatic normative developments in international politics during the past half-century. Yet, recent political events -- from contestation of the International Criminal Court to the election of populist leaders opposed to legal accountability -- have fueled widespread concern that the world is returning to an era of impunity. In this article, we document a sharp global decline in human rights prosecutions since 2010 and develop a theory to explain this trend. We argue that human rights accountability requires a government willing and able to supply justice and a domestic audience that demands it. After 2010, the demand for prosecutions decreased in states with responsive governments and increased in states with the types of governments least likely to supply justice. We test this argument using an original dataset of all international, foreign, and domestic human rights prosecutions initiated between 1970 and 2023. Consistent with our theory, we show that the global shift is driven by a reduction of prosecutions in domestic courts and that together supply and demand factors are strongly predictive of domestic trial initiation. Our argument and findings indicate that the global decline in prosecutions is both a sign of success and a cause for concern. While past legacies of violence were addressed in openings created by democratic transitions, contemporary democratic backsliding risks denying justice to today’s victims.

title: ANALYSIS OF BUDGET MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS IN SUPPORTING PERFORMANCE ACHIEVEMENT OF THE ORGANIZATION FOR EARTH SCIENCES AND MARITIME (ORKM), NATIONAL RESEARCH AND INNOVATION AGENCY
abstract: This report examines the effectiveness of budget management at the Organization for Earth Sciences and Maritime (ORKM), a research organization under Indonesia's National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), during fiscal year 2025. The analysis is motivated by an apparent tension in ORKM's reported figures: a budget realization rate of approximately 87.4% (IDR 11.003 billion against a ceiling of IDR 12.59 billion) coexisted with full achievement of DIPA-funded output targets and a Budget Execution Performance Indicator (IKPA) score of 95.80, categorized "very good." Rather than treating this combination as self-evidently positive, the report interrogates it using document analysis of ORKM's internal planning and performance records (Terms of Reference, Work and Budget Plans, DIPA, and the 2025 Performance Report) together with participatory observation gathered during a practical work placement with ORKM's Program and Finance Team from June 29 to August 29, 2026. Effectiveness is assessed through Duncan's (1973) three-dimensional framework (goal attainment, integration, and adaptation) supplemented by a SWOT analysis to derive development strategies. The findings indicate that ORKM's budget management is effective in a qualified sense: output achievement and inter-document integration are strong, and the organization adapted successfully to shifts in grant disbursement schedules, yet component-level IKPA scores reveal a persistent planning weakness in the correspondence between the Cash Disbursement Plan (RPD) and actual realization, particularly for grant transactions. The report concludes that a single aggregate metric, whether the absorption rate or the IKPA score, is insufficient to characterize budget effectiveness, and recommends that ORKM prioritize strengthening RPD planning accuracy and digitalizing its verification workflow. As an internship-based report grounded in secondary documents and observation rather than primary data collection, the analysis is interpretive in nature and intended as a foundation for further empirical inquiry.

title: The Role of Financial Literacy in Mediating the Influence of BSI Mitraguna on the Growth of MSMEs in Aceh
authors: Yenny Irawan, Diana, Heri Fajri, Mariana, Zahriatul Aini, M Yazid AR
abstract: This study investigates the influence of BSI Mitraguna financing on the development of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Aceh, with particular attention to the role of financial literacy. Using a quantitative explanatory research design, the study focuses on active BSI Mitraguna financing recipients in Aceh. Respondents were selected based on specific criteria, including a minimum duration of financing engagement and ongoing MSME operations. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire using a Likert scale and analyzed using the Structural Equation Modeling--Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) method with SmartPLS software. The results reveal that BSI Mitraguna plays a significant role in fostering MSME growth. It not only provides financial capital but also contributes to improving the financial literacy of MSME actors. Furthermore, financial literacy serves as a crucial intermediary, enhancing the effectiveness of financing in driving business development. These findings suggest that microfinance programs are more impactful when integrated with financial education tailored to the specific needs of local entrepreneurs. Ultimately, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on Islamic microfinance by demonstrating that the synergy between financing and financial literacy is essential for sustainable MSME development. It also provides practical implications for policymakers and financial institutions to design integrated financing models that not only support capital access but also strengthen entrepreneurial capacity, thereby enhancing long-term economic resilience and inclusive growth

title: Distributional Validity and Calibration of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel for Digital and AI Service Use: A Secondary-Data Validation Against the Korea Media Panel Survey
abstract: Synthetic personas based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, yet systematic validation outside English-speaking contexts remains scarce. This secondary-data study evaluates how well a Korean synthetic persona panel (NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-Korea), conditioned into Gemini 3.5 Flash (primary) and EXAONE (comparison), reproduces digital and AI service-use distributions from the KISDI Korea Media Panel Survey. Sex-and-age-stratified panels of about 8,000 personas per model answered the survey's own items - eight service-use indicators and eight innovativeness and acceptance constructs - and were compared against weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE; RQ1) was 15-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.69-0.90. Segment error (RQ2) across five demographic axes was 15-19 pp, with between-group gaps up to 52.4/36.2 pp (Gemini/EXAONE). Errors followed model-specific signatures: an age stereotype with low anchoring (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Reference-year analysis was consistent with temporal misalignment driving most generative-AI overestimation, whereas short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive. Holdout calibration on 30% of the real data (RQ3) roughly halved sex-by-age cell MAE (18.9 to 8.6, 15.9 to 6.7 pp) - yet direct estimation from the same real subsample was far more accurate (3.6 pp), and the correction did not transfer across time. The calibrated panel retained an advantage only under extremely scarce real data (about 100 responses) and, for one model, for unobserved segments. Persona-narrative conditioning beat demographic-only conditioning, but neither surpassed simple real-data baselines. Synthetic panels are thus not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic, with operational use confined to settings lacking real data.

title: Coal Discharge Operations at a State-Owned Rail Logistics Terminal: A Case Study of Process Coordination and Information Flow at PT Kereta Api Indonesia's Tarahan Terminal
abstract: State-owned rail logistics operators in emerging economies face a persistent tension between procedurally mature physical operations and underdeveloped digital coordination infrastructure. This case study examines the coal discharge process at PT Kereta Api Indonesia's (PT KAI) Tarahan Terminal in Lampung, Indonesia, drawing on 30 days of structured participant observation, document analysis, and informal interviews conducted during an internship in the Freight Transport (Angkutan Barang) unit. The discharge cycle—from rangkaian inspection at Tanjung Enim Baru, loading at the Train Loading System, transit to Tarahan, and unloading via the Rotary Car Dumperis mapped end-to-end and evaluated against operations management, supply chain management, and management information systems perspectives. While the physical workflow adheres closely to standard operating procedures and is supported by a structured document chain (Berita Acara Muat, Berita Acara Bongkar, Waktu Peredaran Kereta Api reporting), a SWOT analysis reveals that operational coordination remains dependent on informal, unstructured channels (principally WhatsApp) for transmitting time-sensitive information such as train circulation schedules and equipment-hindrance reports. This creates traceability gaps and latency risk that the formal procedural infrastructure does not, by itself, resolve. The study synthesizes these findings into a SWOT–TOWS strategy matrix and proposes a centralized digital monitoring dashboard alongside a direct-communication protocol (e.g., handheld radio) for time-critical disruptions at the Rotary Car Dumper interface. The case contributes a grounded, practice-level illustration of how digital-transformation and liquidity/resilience logics documented in prior public-sector operations literature (Indrajaya et al., 2026) manifest at the operational front line of a state logistics enterprise and offers actionable recommendations for terminal-level information governance.

title: Standardizing Business Process Documentation for Operational Transition: A Case Study of Employee Administration Data Entry at PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Persero) Tbk
abstract: Organizational transitions that transfer operational activities from internal units to external partners depend heavily on the availability of standardized process documentation. This study examines the business process of Employee Administration (EA) Kedinasan data entry within the Employee & Organization Data Operation (EODO) unit of PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Persero) Tbk, undertaken as part of the company's preparation to transfer data-entry activities to an external partner, PT Infomedia Nusantara. Using a descriptive-qualitative case study approach grounded in Business Process Management (BPM) theory, the study maps the existing (as-is) process through direct observation, documentation review, and discussion with field supervisors, and evaluates it using SWOT analysis to identify internal and external factors shaping the transition. The findings show that although the EA Kedinasan process already possesses a structured workflow supported by verification and approval checkpoints and a centralized SAP-based system, its documentation remains fragmented across multiple work instructions and lacks an integrated reference that can function effectively as a knowledge-transfer medium for an external partner. The study recommends the consolidation of Business Process diagrams, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Work Instructions, and a Playbook into a single coherent documentation package, which was implemented in part during the internship. Beyond its immediate organizational relevance, the case illustrates a broader tension in business process transitions: technically sound processes can still generate transition risk when explicit-knowledge artifacts are not consolidated for an external audience. The study contributes a practitioner-grounded account of how BPM and knowledge-transfer principles operate in a real outsourcing transition within a large Indonesian state-owned enterprise, and offers implications for organizations preparing similar administrative transfers.

title: Media Accountability in the Age of Social Media in Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Omeiza Robinson Ofuje, Ekhareafo, O. Daniel, Daniel Ezegwu
abstract: This study examined media accountability in the age of social media in Nigeria, focusing on the challenges and opportunities presented by digital communication technologies to ethical journalism and professional media practice. Using a library-based research approach, the study draws on books, journal articles, policy documents, media reports and relevant online scholarly materials to critically analyse the evolving accountability landscape within the Nigerian media environment. The study was anchored on Social Responsibility Theory and Accountability Systems Theory. Findings revealed that although Nigerian media institutions and regulatory bodies have made efforts to adapt to digital media through fact-checking initiatives, editorial reforms and policy regulations, significant gaps remain in ensuring ethical compliance, combating misinformation and rebuilding audience trust. The study concludes that strengthening media accountability requires greater commitment to professional ethics, responsible journalism, digital fact-checking, media literacy and robust institutional frameworks that protect freedom of expression while promoting responsible digital communication.

title: HIERARCHICAL METHODOLOGY OF DMYTRO KRIVENKO: THE LIMITS OF DIALECTICS AND LEVELS OF PHYSICAL KNOWLEDGE
abstract: This article reconstructs the philosophical and methodological programme of Dmytro T. Krivenko (1941–1994) as a level-sensitive approach to scientific and philosophical thought. Its historical basis comprises his publications of 1973–1988 on quantitative concepts, informational levels, rational inheritance, and the coarse-graining of complex systems; his 1991 formulation of a “hierarchical model of human cognition”; and manuscripts completed during his lifetime and published posthumously as Prynat i prynatyka (1996). The article argues that Krivenko did not merely add the notion of levels to a universal dialectical scheme. He distinguished the functions of general-philosophical, logical-methodological, and discipline-specific scientific levels. General philosophy could orient inquiry, but it could not replace measurement, mathematical constructions, models, limiting transitions, or empirical testing. Dialectics thereby ceased to operate as a self-sufficient algorithm of cognition and became one possible heuristic instrument within a broader hierarchical methodology. Five central elements of this programme are examined: the formation of physical quantities, informational levels, the growth of informativeness, rational inheritance, and coarse-graining. Scientific development is understood neither as the simple accumulation of facts nor as a universal movement through thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. A successor theory selectively preserves confirmed observations, relations, procedures, and limiting results while changing the ontology and structure of explanation. Coarse-graining shows how knowledge may advance through a controlled loss of detail. The anthropological and political dimension is reconstructed through the concepts of the Prynat and Prynatics. The Prynat is a holistic configuration of three levels of human Nature—the biological, the social or “sociumal,” and the spiritual—together with the individual forms through which they are expressed. All three levels are necessary, but the spiritual has the highest normative status because it integrates biological and social existence with freedom, dignity, and responsibility. Krivenko associates the absolutization of the biological with extreme nationalism and Nazism, the absolutization of the sociumal with communism, and the integrative spiritual level with democracy. Finally, Krivenko’s programme is compared with contemporary discussions of emergence, effective theories, multilevel ontology, and later applications to quark and exploratory preon models. These comparisons are not retrospective attributions, but tests of his central principle: a deeper description is scientifically meaningful only when it preserves validated knowledge, defines its domain of applicability, constructs explicit transitions between levels, yields independent consequences, and remains open to empirical falsification.

title: Spatial mobility and the risk of dropping out of vocational education and training in Germany: Costs, resources, and returns
abstract: Vocational education and training (VET) dropout disrupts school-to-work transitions. While spatial mobility is an important strategy for accessing VET, little is known about how it relates to subsequent dropout. Drawing on a cost-benefit perspective, this study examines whether first-year VET dropout differs by spatial mobility and whether these differences vary with resources available to bear mobility-related costs and returns that may offset them. We use representative longitudinal data from the German National Educational Panel Study linked to administrative geospatial data. Logistic regression models distinguish non-mobile students from those mobile within and between regional labor markets (RLMs) and assess heterogeneity by parental socioeconomic status (SES), VET wages, realized occupational aspirations, regional attractiveness, and regional person-environment match. Predicted dropout probabilities are approximately three percentage points higher for mobility within RLMs and four points higher for mobility between RLMs than for no mobility. These mobility-related differences decrease with increasing parental SES for both mobility types. Higher VET wages correspond to smaller dropout differences for mobility within RLMs, whereas greater realization of occupational aspirations corresponds to smaller differences for mobility between RLMs. Higher regional attractiveness shows a similar pattern only for mobility within RLMs, while higher regional person-environment match coincides with smaller dropout differences for both mobility types. Overall, mobility-related dropout differences vary with available resources and realized returns. The social patterning of mobility-related dropout differences may contribute to inequalities in school-to-work transitions, underscoring the importance of considering spatial mobility and regional contexts in research on youths’ educational decision-making.

title: Toward Interethnic Peace
abstract: General conditions conducive to interethnic peace are examined through the successful experiences of the post-slavery, multiethnic societies of Réunion and Mauritius. Intimacy, openness to others, and solidarity are identified as key characteristics of Creole societies that facilitate the emergence of attributes shared across individuals—a prerequisite for the construction of a harmonious society regardless of skin color. This congruence of values, conceptualized as surface hybridity and represented by the concept of the Creole envelope, was initially fostered by forced miscegenation. It subsequently deepened during the post-emancipation period through growing solidarity in response to recurring hardships, including natural disasters, deadly epidemics, and prolonged economic depression. Because most multiethnic Creole societies did not evolve into peaceful and cohesive communities, we highlight the importance of appropriate political institutions and, more specifically, the central role of human dignity as a foundational value. Drawing inspiration from natural systems and models of collective behavior in both animals and humans, we argue that dignity serves as the linchpin aligning uprooted Creole individuals with common political institutions, which serve as a societal template. Inspired by biomimetic assembly models, we suggest that surface hybridity may constitute a sufficient condition for the emergence of a peaceful and enduring multiethnic society by fostering the convergence of certain values across ethnic groups while preserving their distinctive core values.

title: International development partnerships and nonprofit capacity in Ghana: an integrative review with practitioner evidence
abstract: International development partners route a substantial share of assistance through civil society, yet only a small proportion of this funding reaches organisations based in partner countries directly. This paper asks under what funding and partnership arrangements international support can strengthen Ghanaian nonprofits while preserving local ownership and organisational autonomy. I combine an integrative review of scholarly and policy literature with telephone consultations conducted in July 2026 with representatives of eleven Ghanaian nonprofit organisations using a common set of open-ended questions. The evidence indicates persistent funding volatility, restricted support for institutional costs, barriers to direct grant access, and significant administrative burdens. I argue that support is more likely to strengthen local organisations when it is predictable, reaches the institution as well as the project, uses proportionate access and reporting requirements, and preserves local authority over priorities. Practitioner accounts also locate part of organisational fragility in domestic regulatory and operating conditions that donor reform cannot address. International funding reform and improvements in Ghana's enabling environment therefore need to proceed together.

title: Competency Restoration Timeliness in Washington Under Trueblood 2018-2026
abstract: Objective. A federal court found Washington State's competency-restoration system unconstitutional in 2015 for making defendants found incompetent to stand trial wait months in jail for a psychiatric bed; the State did not appeal that part of the injunction, and the Ninth Circuit left it undisturbed in 2016. The system did not turn around until after years of escalating enforcement culminating in a contempt finding and a $100 million fine. We ask whether that timing reflects sustained federal-court enforcement, and what drove it. Methods. We built an open monthly panel of Washington's Trueblood court-monitor data (January 2018–May 2026; 1,033 rows) and analyzed statewide inpatient restoration timeliness as an interrupted time series against a 7-day admission standard, alongside a jail-based-evaluation comparator on a looser clock. Results. The system was non-compliant for six years (annual median waits 28.0–63.5 days; compliance rarely above 30%, and 6% in March 2023 when the median wait peaked at 97 days), then improved sharply — median 5.0 days, 90.4% average compliance, holding over 26 months of continued oversight. The gain concentrated in bed-dependent services: both moved sharply while the bed-independent comparator's median wait moved +0.0 days on the raw split and a small but statistically significant −1.3 days on the regression estimator; coding by Washington's Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) attributes an average 90.8% of restoration delays to bed availability, though almost all of that coding predates the turnaround. All facilities improved; demand rose, not fell (Limitations). Conclusions. The improvement coincided with sustained Trueblood enforcement; this single-jurisdiction design supports association, not causation. The open, re-executable panel offers an independent compliance monitor complementary to the state's own.

title: Good jobs, bad jobs, and the upward mobility potential of self-employment
abstract: Most of the self-employed eventually return to paid employment. Prior research documents a penalty for former entrepreneurs re-entering paid employment but assumes a background of a standard job. Could entrepreneurship facilitate upward mobility for workers from casual employment backgrounds instead? For these workers, entrepreneurship can demonstrate previously hidden ability through observable business performance and provide them with a more stable base from which to seek standard employment. I investigate the earnings and employment trajectories of former entrepreneurs in India. Among those who previously worked in non-salaried employment, those with a short spell in self-employment experience a small penalty. Those with a longer, successful spell reap large earnings premiums and transition to salaried employment at higher rates than matched controls. In contrast, most former entrepreneurs from salaried backgrounds face persistent earnings penalties. These results reveal how the upward mobility potential of entrepreneurship depends on alternative employment options. By relaxing assumptions of stable employment backgrounds, this study extends the careers lens to the modal entrepreneur globally.

title: Sense of place based on shared imaginaries for caring for the chinampa socio‑ecosystem
authors: Ana Paula Margain Leon, Lakshmi Charli Joseph, Jesús Mario Siqueiros-Garcia
abstract: Sense of place refers to the meaningful connection that people establish with a space, which can either motivate or inhibit environmental care. Understanding the mechanisms that strengthen this connection is central to promoting sustainable ways of cohabiting a place. This study proposes imagining desired futures as a mechanism to mobilise a sense of place among young people from Xochimilco in Mexico City and to catalyse new forms of care. Drawing on a qualitative methodology, the study shows that this connection became a conscious, deliberate act that enabled reflection and collective visibility of bonds with place. The findings suggest that imagining futures expands the possibilities for collective care.

title: The Institutional Production of Causation: Predictive Classification and the Limits of Self-Attested Transparency in AI Governance
abstract: Predictive classifications do not merely describe the world. Once embedded in institutional decisions, they alter access, scrutiny, opportunity and the evidence from which their own validity is later assessed. This Perspective extends that account of institutional causation to the governance of AI systems. Providers and oversight bodies classify incidents as authorised or unauthorised, material or immaterial, in scope or out of scope, and verified or unverified. These labels allocate investigative attention and determine which records are preserved, which populations are examined and which explanations remain available. When the institution issuing a classification also controls the evidence capable of testing it, a closed evidentiary loop can result: the initial category defines the inquiry, the inquiry defines the evidence population, and that population ratifies the category. Detailed disclosure may then remain self-attested rather than independently verifiable. The discovery disputes in The New York Times Company v. Microsoft Corporation et al. illustrate the institutional difference between disclosure and contestability. Court-ordered preservation, negotiated sampling, de-identification and controlled access did not decide the merits of the litigation, but they created an external forum in which evidence scope and negative assurances could be challenged. Transparent AI governance therefore requires more than publication. It requires institutional separation between the authority to classify and the authority to determine what evidence may test the classification.

title: Making Sense of Machines: Ritualized Care, Agency Attribution, and Failure Interpretation in Human-Automation Encounters in India
abstract: Machines in India are cared for, spoken to, honored, and blamed, well beyond ordinary use. New vehicles are blessed before their first drive, workshop tools are garlanded and rested during Vishwakarma Puja, and small tilak marks or deity images sit on machine casings without a second thought. Human-computer and human-robot interaction research has rarely asked what these everyday practices do to the way people read a machine that hesitates, fails, or behaves unexpectedly. This paper reports a formative, mixed-method study of how adults in India make sense of ambiguous automated behavior, and whether caring for and personifying machines shapes how they read that behavior. A survey of 156 adults gives a baseline for how common these practices are, how people explain failure, how much agency they grant a machine, and what they want from a system when it fails. Machine-care practices turned out to be almost universal: 96% of respondents reported at least one. In a scenario where a vehicle fails before an important journey and then starts again on its own, 62% chose a relational or meaningful explanation alongside the technical option they were also given, and 60% expected a machine they had looked after to perform well in return. The interviews complicate that last figure: most of what looks like relational trust there is closer to an ordinary belief that upkeep improves performance. The orientation toward the recovering vehicle did not carry over evenly to newer technology, either. About a third of respondents said they trusted AI more than mechanical machines and expected it to “know better,” a view far more common among younger respondents. I read the survey alongside twenty-one semi-structured interviews, conducted in Hindi and English with photographs and short scenarios and analyzed thematically. Across both urban and rural lives, people mostly treated machine care as ordinary maintenance, not as a belief that machines are conscious. That relational orientation showed up again and again, but it also ran into real limits: in platform work, in closed or inaccessible design, and among people who reject it on rational or minority-faith grounds. There is no single Indian view of machines here. Region, generation, religion, and class produce real differences, and I treat those differences as central to the findings, not as noise to explain away. The paper offers three things: a documented instrument set for studying culturally situated automation sensemaking, along with an honest account of where its measures blur together and how they could be sharpened; a preliminary vocabulary connecting ritualized care, agency attribution, and failure interpretation; and an early design agenda for settings where machines carry meaning beyond what they do.

title: Beyond Prediction Error: A Decision-Theoretic Model of Resistance to Belief Updating
abstract: Agents often decline to adopt revisions their own inference supports. We propose that posterior computation and belief implementation are distinct operations: Bayesian inference produces candidate revisions, and a cost-sensitive decision — an endorsement gate — determines whether a revision becomes the operative belief, P(U = 1) = σ(β₀ + β_E·E − β_C·C), with E the posterior displacement (Bayesian surprise) and C the expected reorganization cost of implementation. The model adds a gating layer between inference and representational change without modifying inference. We derive the logistic implementation probability conditional on a specified random-utility representation, give a dynamic formulation with partial updating, and evaluate parameter recovery, estimator behavior, and rival discrimination across a reproducible simulation programme spanning identifiability, estimator pathology and correction, rival discrimination, adversarial severity, and design calibration, with four formal analyses. The theory’s confirmatory content is one preregistered discriminative program with two logically ordered stages, formalized as fixed-sequence gatekeeping. Stage one — state-trace coupling under selective single-channel cost manipulation — separates the gate from independent channelwise commitment thresholds: a reversed, two-dimensional association is fatal. Stage two — content-specificity in a matched-displacement, within-class two-belief design — separates a content-bearing operative state from content-general or content-conditioned threshold policies: a certified null belief-by-cost interaction is fatal, as is content-specific staleness without an implicit–downstream gap, or a positive pattern that retrieval probes expose as trace competition. An identity-conditioned threshold policy is shown to be observationally and psychofunctionally equivalent to the gate under a representationalist construal — underdetermination of ontology, not the victory of one vocabulary — so the empirical content rides on the shared structure. A severity-gated verdict table fixes in advance which outcomes are fatal, which supportive, and which merely silent. Every claim is flagged confirmatory or interpretive; alternatives are organized by a working taxonomy — empirical rivals, equivalent redescriptions, artifact families — whose placements are functional for the program, not verdicts on any account’s standing as a theory. The program opens with a pre-Stage-1 validation pilot whose success criteria are measurement properties, never effects, gated by preregistered traffic-light progression criteria. The register is held fixed throughout: a successful future experiment could support, at best, a shared, channel-coupled, content-specific, use-level operative constraint on belief use; the endorsement gate is the most parsimonious interpretation of that structure, and the choice of interpretive vocabulary is downstream of the result, not part of it.

title: The development of subsistence effort and skill among BaYaka foragers
authors: Sheina Lew-Levy, Erik Ringen, Lucie Benoit, Yann R. Ouamba, Adam Boyette, Sarah Pope-Caldwell, Lee Gettler, Alyssa N. Crittenden
abstract: Why humans have such long childhoods is an evolutionary puzzle. Childhood may represent a developmental period for the acquisition of cognitive and physical skills needed to exploit the complex hunted and gathered resources typical of our species’ subsistence niche. Childhood may also be an extended period for cooperating with kin, and by extension, reaping inclusive fitness benefits. Studies in contemporary hunter-gatherer communities show that subsistence proficiency peaks in adulthood. Yet, there is considerable inter-individual variation in food returns, with some children efficiently collecting specific resources from a young age, and others exceeding their daily caloric needs. To understand why some children are more productive than others, here we investigate the association between subsistence effort and skill development among Congo Basin BaYaka foragers. BaYaka rely on hunting, gathering, fishing, and small-scale horticulture for subsistence. We measured subsistence effort and food production over a six-week period in a forest camp with 52 residents aged 0 to 70 years. We analyzed these data using a Bayesian latent hierarchical model. We found that 50% of subsistence skill was achieved by age 15. Both subsistence skill and effort peaked in adulthood. Further, we found a negative age-adjusted correlation between effort and skill, suggesting that lower-skilled individuals participated in subsistence more frequently. Overall, our findings show that children can meaningfully reduce day-to-day dependence on adults, which over evolutionary time, may have helped offset the cost of extended human childhood.

title: Determinants of Patent Applications across European Regions: Evidence from Panel Estimators, K-Means Clustering and Predictive Validation
