authors: Angelo Maurizio Galiano, Giuseppe Dell'Erba, Alberto Costantiello, Angelo Leogrande
abstract: Europe measures the innovative performance of its regions largely by counting patents, and allocates public resources accordingly. This paper asks what regional patenting actually reflects, drawing on Regional Innovation Scoreboard data for 245 European regions observed annually between 2016 and 2023. Three candidate drivers are considered: the research effort of firms, the intensity of formal collaboration between the research base and industry, and the propensity to protect intangible assets through trademarks. Business research effort emerges as the dominant correlate throughout, science–industry collaboration as a weaker but consistent one, and trademark activity as a positive one, suggesting that firms which protect brands are not forgoing patents but exercising a single appropriation capability across several instruments. Two findings carry implications beyond measurement. Regional innovative capacity proves remarkably immobile: differences between regions account for roughly 95 per cent of the variation in the data, and differences within a region over the eight years for the remainder, so the short-run movements on which policy evaluation typically relies carry very little information, and the returns to innovation investment should be sought over horizons far longer than a programming cycle. And when the 245 regions are grouped into four innovation profiles rather than treated as a single population, the relationship that holds on average holds almost nowhere in particular: it is strong among leading and lagging regions, statistically absent in the largest group, and displaced by brand-led appropriation in a fourth group of 27 regions whose innovation is real but largely non-technological. Uniform innovation policy prescriptions and uniform managerial benchmarks are correspondingly difficult to justify.

title: Beyond the Rural Designation: Geographic Aggregation as a Justice Problem in Psychiatric–Mental Health Nursing
abstract: Objective: To argue that the geographic category "rural," as operationalized in disparities research and federal shortage-area designation, conceals the rural populations who fare worst, and what follows for psychiatric–mental health (PMH) nursing. Methods: Critical analysis of literature on rural mental health disparities, rurality measurement, and racially and sexually minoritized rural populations, spanning 2002, when the field was urged past counting rural disorder toward how place shapes it, through 2026. Results: Prevalence findings have stayed inconsistent for two decades, substantially because rurality is measured dichotomously. On disaggregation, the rural–urban axis often proves the wrong one: among American Indian and Alaska Native veterans, urban–rural comparison yields no significant difference while comparison with White veterans yields large ones. Because shortage-area designation is geographic, the aggregate does not merely describe disparity; it drives allocation. Conclusions: Aggregation is not a neutral convenience. A category that renders the worst-off invisible and governs resource distribution is a justice concern for a specialty supplying much of rural America's mental health workforce. PMH nursing should assess structural position rather than residence, adopt continuous and intersectional measures of rurality, and contest designation methodology as professional advocacy.

title: Love at First Swipe: Online Dating and Relationship Outcomes in Europe
abstract: This article examines whether unions formed through online dating differ from other unions in relationship trajectories across nine European countries. Using harmonised Generations and Gender Survey data, I estimate country-specific survival and current-union models for union dissolution, marriage, shared biological childbearing, relationship satisfaction, and break-up consideration. Adjusted dissolution hazards are higher in Austria, Estonia, and Croatia, lower in Germany, and not significant elsewhere or among recent unions. Among surviving unions, online dating is more often associated with lower marriage and shared childbearing, especially in Croatia and the United Kingdom, than with poorer relationship quality. Overall, online dating appears more strongly associated with how unions are institutionalised and converted into family life and the findings do not support the idea of a uniform pan-European relationship difference associated with online dating.

title: Governments as Adopters and Regulators of AI: A Challenge for Democracy?
abstract: This paper explores the dual role of governments as both adopters and regulators of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on the implications for democratic governance. As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in public administration – from policymaking to service delivery – they offer opportunities for improving efficiency and personalization but also raise concerns about transparency, accountability, and fairness. To deal with these questions, this paper examines how AI is framed as a policy problem, the regulatory approaches adopted in different political systems, and the politicization of AI governance. It also analyzes the democratic risks posed by algorithmic decision-making, polarization, and corporate concentration of power, while highlighting the potential of AI to enhance democratic quality through improved public services, inclusive discourse, and citizen engagement. The paper concludes by identifying key areas for future research, including legitimacy, trust, regulatory design, and equity in AI governance.

title: Optimizing Recovery Value in Public Asset Disposal: Business Process Mapping (As-Is vs. To-Be) Analysis of State-Owned Asset Sales and Write-Offs at Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs
abstract: Efficient management of state-owned assets (Barang Milik Negara, BMN) is a critical determinant of fiscal accountability and non-tax state revenue (Penerimaan Negara Bukan Pajak, PNBP) optimization in public sector organizations. This study examines the process of proposing, verifying, and executing the sale and write-off of low-value BMN (below IDR 100 million) at the Bureau of Finance and State Assets, Secretariat General, Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (KOMDIGI), where delegated approval authority under Minister of Finance Regulation (PMK) No. 4/PMK.06/2015 was, in practice, insufficiently leveraged to accelerate administrative throughput. Employing a qualitative, participant-observation-based case study design conducted over a six-week practicum period, this research applies Business Process Mapping (As-Is vs. To-Be) to document the existing workflow, identify bottlenecks and non-value-added activities, and design a redesigned process architecture. The As-Is analysis reveals three structural inefficiencies: (1) duplicated manual verification between spreadsheet-based checklists and the State Asset Management Information System (SIMAN); (2) recurrent data mismatches across unit nomenclature, asset codes, and book values; and (3) an undifferentiated verification pathway that fails to exploit the risk-based delegation of authority for low-value assets. A SWOT matrix further situates these findings within the organization's internal capabilities and external opportunities, generating SO, WO, ST, and WT strategic alternatives. The proposed To-Be process (anchored on system integration, a risk-based fast-track lane, and standardized correspondence templates) is theorized to compress processing lead time and thereby preserve the economic value of assets pending disposal, directly reinforcing recovery value and PNBP contributions. This study contributes to the limited empirical literature on business process reengineering in Indonesian public asset governance and offers a replicable diagnostic-to-design framework for other line ministries operating under similarly delegated regulatory regimes.

title: Measuring and Repairing Document Conversion Errors in the Michigan Child Welfare Policy Manual
abstract: Author Note (August 18, 2026): This preprint is currently undergoing systematic review and revision. An updated version will be posted upon completion. Readers are encouraged to consult the latest version of the manuscript. Child welfare practice is governed by documents written for people to read. A state policy manual specifies how quickly a caseworker must see a child after the child returns home, and it does so in a PDF laid out for the eye. Any system that answers questions from such a manual must first convert it into text, and that conversion step is rarely measured. This study measures it. Five test documents were constructed to replicate the layout of the Michigan Children’s Protective Services Manual, with identifiers replacing its words. The identifiers run consecutively, so that a loss reads as a gap in a counted run and a person can see it without tooling, and each one ends in a check code, so that a converter driven by a language model cannot supply a convincing replacement for whatever it dropped. The same artifact is therefore verifiable by a person reading it and by a script counting it, and the tool under test cannot repair the evidence before either of them looks at it. Four converters were evaluated on the test documents, and the two generations of the commercial service were evaluated on the manual itself, for a total of 31 documents and 328 pages. No converter was adequate for every property required by a retrieval corpus. The older generation invented 43 section headings that appear nowhere in the source, and the corpus assembled from it labels a column in a contact-standards table with the wrong requirement, so it lists three contacts with each child at intensive risk, where the manual states one. The current generation’s cheapest tier deletes the opening line of every paragraph beginning Exception:, which is how this manual marks the cases a rule does not cover. None of these failures garbles the text. Each produces fluent prose that reads as policy and states a rule the manual does not contain. The study then reports a repair procedure that derives document structure from the PDF’s geometry, and fifteen checks that halt conversion if any fail. Every check passes across all 31 documents, measured against the same documents from which the repair rules were derived. A fourth failure property emerged only after presence, level, and order had all reached their best values: 380 paragraph boundaries across 200 of the 328 pages were marked in the source by vertical spacing that the converter does not read.

title: Financial Risk Management Practices in a State-Owned Energy Enterprise: A Process-Based Case Study of Market Research Operations at PT Pertamina (Persero)
abstract: Financial risk management (FRM) has become a strategic function within state-owned energy enterprises exposed to volatile commodity prices, exchange rate fluctuations, and interest rate movements. While a substantial body of literature examines the determinants and firm-level consequences of financial risk exposure and hedging behavior, comparatively little empirical or practice-based work documents how such risk-monitoring functions are operationally structured and executed within large state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in emerging markets. This study addresses that gap through a process-based case study of the Market Research sub-function within the Financial Risk & Insurance Center (FRIC) of PT Pertamina (Persero), Indonesia's national energy company. Using Business Process Modeling (BPM) with BPMN notation and a SWOT analysis supported by Internal Factor Analysis Summary (IFAS) and External Factor Analysis Summary (EFAS) matrices, this study maps the daily workflow of market monitoring and Morning Market Flash Report preparation, identifies operational strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, and formulates strategic recommendations. The findings indicate that the process exhibits strong internal verification controls (a multi-tier review chain and the use of integrated tools such as Bloomberg Terminal and the FRAME application) but remains constrained by manual data-entry processes and tight pre-market deadlines. Positioned in Quadrant I (Growth/SO) of the SWOT matrix, the function is well placed to pursue an aggressive strategy centered on automation and standardization. The study contributes a practice-grounded account of financial risk monitoring operations that complements the predominantly econometric literature on FRM determinants and offers actionable recommendations for both corporate practice and academic curricula in financial risk education.

title: From Search Engines to Answer Engines: Testing the Effects of Traditional and AI Search Engines on Belief in Misinformation
authors: Kylan Rutherford, Zeve Sanderson, Jonathan Nagler, Joshua A. Tucker
abstract: Counter to the advice in many digital literacy guides, recent research has demonstrated that using a search engine to learn more about false or misleading articles can actually incorrectly increase belief in the veracity of that news (Aslett et al. 2024). As the future of search turns to AI-powered search and chatbots, will AI be able to ameliorate this problem? To investigate this question, we recruited over 4,000 participants to assess the veracity of recent news articles, and evaluate how using either a traditional search engine (TSE) or an AI search engine (AISE) affects their assessments. We find that using the AISE (Perplexity) increases belief in misinformation at almost the same rate as the TSE (Google). We also find that search strategies which perform poorly on TSEs (e.g., copying and pasting links) may actually improve the utility of AISEs. We find no difference in the rate of unreliable links served.

title: Political Talk in Nonpolitical Digital Spaces
abstract: In recent years, scholars in communication and media studies have increasingly turned their attention to political discourse that emerges incidentally within ostensibly nonpolitical digital contexts. These political discussions not only permeate diverse online platforms and communities, but also carry significant democratic potential. Despite growing interest in the phenomenon, existing research remains fragmented across distinct theoretical traditions and lacks a coherent conceptual understanding. This article addresses that gap by reviewing studies in three epistemological orientations—post-positivist, interpretive, and critical—that can guide the analysis of political talk in nonpolitical digital environments. In doing so, it highlights how this group of phenomena can be understood and interpreted with different theoretical assumptions, thereby enabling scholars to better assess their communicative and political significance. This review offers a foundation for more integrative and theoretically informed research on the various dimensions of political expression in digital networked publics.

title: Determinants of Wealth Inequality in the Game of Diplomacy: An economic and computational perspective
authors: Julia Wlodarczyk, Andrew Zadrozny, Kripa Rajshekhar, Wlodek Zadrozny
abstract: This paper presents the first comprehensive analysis of wealth inequality within the strategic game of Diplomacy, addressing a significant gap in existing literature, which typically focuses on tactics, cooperation, and deception rather than distributional outcomes. Utilizing an anonymized dataset of over 1 million records corresponding to players’ winnings (supply centers and all territories) at the end of the game, we calculate Gini coefficients to quantify inequality. The analysis reveals that Diplomacy exhibits moderate-to-high inequality (Gini = 0.56 for supply centers and 0.52 for all territories), comparable to real-world economies such as Spain or South Korea. Fractional logit and beta regressions reveal that wealth inequality in strategic environments is not merely a result of individual skills but is structurally shaped by institutional rules, communication, and path-dependent accumulation. In particular, higher player count and longer game duration are associated with increased inequality. Moreover, the possibility to engage in private communication significantly in- creases wealth disparities compared to no-communication environments, as it facilitates complex coali- tions and betrayals. However, high levels of overall communication activity tend to reduce inequality, though inequality in communication itself (dominance by one speaker) correlates positively with wealth inequality at the end of the game. Finally, preliminary results suggest the presence of AI agents has a significant impact on wealth distribution, confirming that Diplomacy is a relevant laboratory for studying human-AI collaboration and competition

title: Local-Oriented Online Communities in Urban Communication Infrastructures: News Media, Engagement, and Emotion in 128 North American City Communities
abstract: Local-oriented online communities (LOOCs) have become ubiquitous spaces for discussing national and local news as well as urban civic life, yet existing scholarship lacks a consistent framework to explain what shapes their behavioral and emotional outcomes across diverse contexts. This study applies Communication Infrastructure Theory (CIT) to conceptualize LOOCs as meso-level storytellers whose outcomes are shaped by their connections to broader storytelling networks. Analyzing 1,613,650 posts and 32,706,953 comments from 128 North American city subreddits over the full year of 2024, we examine how connections to mainstream media, local media, urban governance topics, and everyday urban life topics predict thread-level engagement and emotional expression. Results show that both mainstream and local media connections substantially increase engagement but correlate with more negative emotional expression. Urban governance topics increase behavioral engagement but elicit negative sentiment, whereas everyday urban life topics exhibit the inverse pattern, showing an engagement–negativity tradeoff.

title: The Dynamics of LGBTQ+ Visibility and Demographic Shifts in the Philippines: A Sociological and Public Health Analysis
abstract: The contemporary demographic landscape of the Philippines has witnessed a significant increase in the visible population of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ+) individuals. Often colloquially and inaccurately characterized as an "overgrowth," this phenomenon represents a complex sociodemographic shift driven by heightened self-identification, evolving sociolinguistic frameworks, and progressive, albeit localized, policy environments. This comprehensive research report examines the multifaceted dimensions of LGBTQ+ population dynamics in the Philippines. Drawing upon national demographic surveys, sociological ethnographies, public health registries, and legal jurisprudence, the analysis deconstructs the mechanisms behind the increased visibility of sexual and gender minorities. The report investigates the profound public health challenges accompanying this demographic shift, specifically the escalating HIV/AIDS epidemic and pervasive mental health crises driven by minority stress. Furthermore, it explores the legislative stagnation of national anti-discrimination protections, the compensatory rise of local government ordinances, and the cultural integration of queer identity through linguistic innovations such as Swardspeak. Ultimately, the evidence suggests that the expanding LGBTQ+ population in the Philippines is not a sudden biological anomaly, but rather a sociological reclamation of space within a society navigating the tension between deeply entrenched post-colonial Abrahamic conservatism and pre-colonial traditions of gender fluidity.

title: If it bleeds, it leads? Evaluating whether LLMs can identify what is newsworthy
abstract: Journalists have always had to make the challenging decision about which stories to focus on and which stories to ignore. This paper investigates whether AI can assist journalists in identifying newsworthy stories from large databases. We first build a dataset of Canadian lobbying registrations, each labeled as "newsworthy" or "not newsworthy" based on whether a journalist covered it in a published article or not. We then systematically evaluate several AI models' ability to identify the one newsworthy registration within a batch of ten. The best models identify a single newsworthy registration with 22% accuracy, rising to 48% when allowed to select three, and to 52% when provided previous headline examples. Our results suggest that a filtering approach silently discards real stories, whereas allowing the model to rank registrations by newsworthiness ensures no information is lost. We conclude that while AI holds real potential to help identify leads, this is not possible without further investment in evaluation infrastructure, and even then, there is an important role for journalists to identify what AI misses, as it cannot replace their editorial judgment entirely.

title: Counting the Accountability Gap: A National Freedom of Information Census of Public Clock Maintenance in England
abstract: Who is responsible for a stopped public clock? This paper reports a national attempt to answer that question empirically, and argues that the pattern of non-answers is itself the finding. Two datasets were assembled. The first is a documented set of 402 stopped public clocks in Britain, collected by field observation and public contribution since 2007 and classified by current custodian; it is a floor, not a census. The second is a census of what English principal councils themselves know: Freedom of Information requests to all 314 principal local authorities, yielding 310 responses of which 187 were substantive, disclosing 566 council-managed clocks of which 70 (12.4%) were stopped. Of the documented set, only 26.4% stand on council-owned buildings, the one category where the Freedom of Information Act compels an answer about maintenance; roughly 74% stand on private, commercial, ecclesiastical or trust-owned buildings, beyond the reach of any public enquiry mechanism. I call this the accountability gap, and I present it strictly as a claim about reach, not cause: for three-quarters of documented failures, a citizen cannot even discover whose job the maintenance was. Direct approaches to some sixty private owners, met overwhelmingly with silence, corroborate the gap from the other side. The stopped public clock is proposed as a countable, photographable proxy for the dissolution of collective maintenance arrangements in the public realm, and the method as a replicable template for measuring accountability reach over any distributed class of shared assets.

title: Agricultural technology and diversification to mitigate climate change-related issues in Chinese rice production: A farmers’ perspective
authors: Qianqian Liu, Estelle Raveloaritiana, Xiaohan Huang, Xueqing He, ZengRong Zhu, Lei Wang, Thomas Cherico Wanger
abstract: Agricultural technology (agri-technology) and diversification (agri-diversification) can advance sustainable agriculture and food security amid climate change, and combining them may amplify benefits. Yet farmers' knowledge and adoption remain poorly understood, limiting scalability. Here, we interviewed 1,352 rice farmers across three Chinese provinces spanning a climatic gradient. Farmers perceived climate change-related challenges mainly as production issues, with 82% reporting rising pest occurrence and 42% reporting health issues. Four of five agri-technology categories were both well known and widely adopted (>91% and >61%, respectively). By contrast, only three of seven agri-diversification categories were widely known (>64%), with most practices below 25% awareness. County-level factors—temperature, per capita gross domestic product and farmland fragmentation—were associated with awareness and adoption for many agri-diversification practices but few agri-technologies. Agri-diversification therefore remains under-recognized and underused, and depends more on local conditions than agri-technology. Targeted policy should promote the co-benefits of implementing both strategies together.

title: Broad Fiscal Burden in Asian Energy-Transition Contexts: How Development Levels Condition Growth
abstract: Asian economies face the challenge of reducing emissions while sustaining economic growth, yet the growth implications of environmental taxation remain uncertain. This study examines whether broad tax burden and energy-system conditions are associated with economic growth in Asia, whether the tax-growth relationship varies by development level, and whether renewable-energy context is more closely related to growth or environmental performance. Using an unbalanced country-year panel of 20 Asian economies from 1972 to 2024, the analysis applies fixed-effects regressions with country and year effects and country-clustered standard errors. Because direct energy-tax measures are unavailable, tax revenue as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) is used as a broad fiscal proxy. The baseline model shows no statistically significant relationship between tax revenue and real gross domestic product per capita growth, while the estimated coefficient is small and negative. Income-group models suggest heterogeneity around this weak average association: the tax-growth relationship is negative for lower-middle-income economies but positive for upper-middle-income and high-income economies. Renewable-energy share does not significantly moderate the tax-growth relationship, but it is strongly associated with lower carbon intensity of output. These findings indicate that taxation’s growth associations depend on development level and not uniform across Asia, while environmental performance is more clearly linked to energy-system structure than to tax revenue alone. Policy should therefore avoid stand- alone tax instruments, pair fiscal reform with revenue recycling and household protection, and expand renewable-energy infrastructure.

title: Cumulative Advantage in Job Quality: Career Trajectories and Inequality in Sweden, 1968–2022
abstract: Cumulative (dis)advantage is well documented for wages and occupational prestige, but whether similar patterns characterize non-monetary working conditions remains unclear. This study examines career trajectories in job quality—job complexity, physical demands, negative stress, and flexibility—using Swedish Level-of-Living Survey panel data from 1968 to 2022 (5,042 respondents; 14,857 observations). We ask whether inequalities in job quality widen or narrow across career stages, whether social groups differ in within-career change, and whether workers who begin from more favorable positions subsequently gain more or less. We estimate adjusted inequalities across career stages using random-slope growth curve models and differences in within-career change using individual fixed-effects models. Job quality generally improved over the first 20–25 career years among cohorts born from the 1940s onward. Educational inequality was large and persistent: workers with more education held better jobs throughout and gained more within their careers. Gender inequality emerged over time: men and women began near parity, but men gained more. Within social groups, however, workers who started with better job quality improved less, indicating convergence. Adjusting for occupation reduced career-stage inequalities more than differences in within-career change. Thus, inequalities may widen between social groups even as differences within groups narrow over the career.

title: Reversal of the Educational Gender Gap and Assortative Mating: Increasing Educational Hypogamy amid Persistent Age Sorting in Latin America
abstract: Previous research has revealed a positive association between female educational advantage and the prevalence of educational hypogamy. However, age assortative mating, as a relevant feature in the process of union formation, has been overlooked. This study analyzes the effect of the decrease of the educational gender gap on the likelihood of being married and age and educational assortative mating among Latin American women. Data come from the harmonized microdata samples from the census rounds of eight Latin American countries from 1970 to 2010, available in the Integrated Public Use of Microdata Series International database. Binomial and multinomial logistic regressions were used to evaluate the effects of changes in the educational gender gap on the odds of being single and being assortatively mated in terms of age and education. Results suggest that changes of the educational gender gap had a negative effect on the probabilities of being married and they were associated with higher levels of educational hypogamy, whereas the patterns of age sorting were more rigid than the patterns of educational sorting.

title: Comparing Information Disorder Policy: The Global Disinformation Policy Database, 2000–2023
abstract: Comparative research on information disorder policy faces a dependent-variable problem: policies sharing a label differ in what they regulate, and policies regulating the same conduct carry different labels. The Global Disinformation Policy Database (GDPD) addresses this problem, coding 364 policies from 132 countries, 2000–2023, and decomposing each into label, information quality, regulated behavior, and intent standard. The decomposition shows that 57.7% of “disinformation” policies specify no intent standard, that policy growth predates the literature’s 2016 watershed, and that instruments have diversified away from criminal sanction along regional lines. The GDPD enables researchers to compare how governments conceptualize contested information.

title: Increases in national origin disparities in ICE Arrests, 2025-26
authors: Caitlin C Patler, Claire Morton, Avi Feller
abstract: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has rapidly expanded operations since the January 2025 US presidential inauguration, raising concerns about profiling based on national origin or ethnicity. We assess this issue using administrative records on nearly 500,000 ICE arrests from November 2023 to March 2026, comparing per-capita arrest rates for unauthorized residents from Europe, Canada, and Oceania (EUCA) with those from all other regions (non-EUCA) in 2025-2026, relative to 2023-2024. We document two patterns that are inconsistent with claims of neutral enforcement. First, non-EUCA per-capita arrest rates rose substantially more than EUCA rates in the 14 months following the inauguration, both nationally as well as in every state and ICE jurisdiction with sufficient data. We estimate 217,000 excess non-EUCA arrests relative to a baseline scenario in which non-EUCA and EUCA arrest rates rose equally. Second, the largest disparities occurred among individuals without convictions apprehended in the community rather than via transfers from criminal custody, contrary to claims of targeting people with criminal records. Together, our findings document pervasive national origin differences in ICE enforcement at a time of acute legal and policy contention, raising new questions about the causes and consequences of these broad disparities.

title: Delisting without co-migration: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
abstract: Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals’ subsequent delisting. Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted-journal event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and administrative coverage-change exits. Findings: Across 136 stacks, delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less that references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a difference that predated delisting. The highest inflow quartile had 4.66 times the adjusted hazard of the lowest (95% CI [2.04, 10.64]), based on 78 events and 99.3% censoring. Research limitations: Delisting is non-random, so estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations. Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it distinguishes the event-defined population. Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion

title: European and US companies communicate less about diversity post-Trump election
authors: Loureiro Lopes, A.I. (Ana Isabel), João Gonçalves
abstract: We analyzed the social media posts of top 20 European and US companies for their Diversity related content before (2024) and after (2025) the election of Donald Trump. We find that there was a decline in diversity related content in 2025 both in the US and in Europe, with the biggest drop being registered in the US. From all social media content, 6,7% of posts by US based companies in 2024 included diversity related topics, while in 2025 only 1,3% were about diversity. For European companies, the scenario is similar. In 2024, 12,6% of social media posts by European companies touch upon diversity content which dropped to 7,0% in the same period of 2025. In general, European companies posted more on diversity than American companies both in 2024 and in 2025. These results show us that while the drop in diversity related talk by corporations was more accentuated in the US, other geographies seem to also replicate the trend.

title: Integrating Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) in Participatory Research Practice with Young Children with Disabilities. A Scoping Review.
abstract: Objective: Young children with disabilities often face barriers to participation in research, as many of them do not use verbal speech. This limits the representation of their views concerning designing research processes, policies, support systems or education. Assuming that the integration of Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) into research methods could be a suitable approach to deconstruct these barriers, this review explores the implementation of AAC into participatory research with this group. Method: A scoping review was conducted (Tricco et al., 2018). Following a systematic search in scientific databases and two screening rounds, 8 studies were included. Full texts were analysed concerning the use of AAC and the modalities of children’s communication by means of Qualitative Content Analysis (Kuckartz & Rädiker, 2024). Results: Only three studies reported unaided or low-tech AAC-use for data collection. Additionally, a wide range of other child-friendly modalities for children to express themselves were identified which facilitated communication, but did not classify as AAC. These strategies were mostly applied during data collection (e.g. within interviews), while decision-making concerning the research process (e.g. choosing a research question of methods) relied on verbal communication. Conclusion: The potential of AAC for participatory research has not yet been realized to its maximum. Nevertheless, other multimodal and child-friendly forms of facilitating children’s communication also are very valuable. Both forms should be extended to support children’s decision-making concerning the research process. Future research should focus on using this potential to involve all children – including those with disabilities - into participatory research.

title: The Geography of Life Chances and Intergenerational Mobility
abstract: We have entered a new era of soaring inequalities in income and wealth, patterns driven by a highly differentiated landscape of opportunity. This economic reality has propelled the geographies of intergenerational mobility and life chances to the forefront of the social science agenda. While geographers are increasingly engaging with these topics, the field of economic geography provides a critical, yet underutilized, theoretical foundation for this work. This chapter proposes the People-Experience-Places (PEP) framework, a model for analyzing the geographic differentiation of life chances across space and time. Drawing from core schools of thought within economic geography, the framework identifies the foundational mechanisms that produce spatially differentiated opportunity regimes and their impact on intergenerational mobility. The chapter concludes with a call for economic geographers to return to the core concerns of understanding and addressing inequalities in livelihood possibilities.

title: A good climate for solutions? The adaptation of solutions journalism within Surinamese climate journalism
abstract: This study explores how climate journalists’ role conceptions and media system constraints shape their perceptions and practices of solutions journalism. It does so through a reflexive thematic analysis of in-depth interviews with five of the six practicing climate journalists in Suriname. Findings suggest that journalists express concerns about environmental injustices, particularly those affecting Indigenous communities, yet remain reluctant to adopt interventionist roles. They define their primary task as informing and providing context rather than promoting specific solutions, with objectivity functioning as a professional norm and strategic resource in a fragile media environment where access to sources is precarious. Solutions journalism is further reinterpreted in the Surinamese context, with solutions only introduced after problems have been thoroughly portrayed. Overall, the findings suggest that professional role conceptualizations and solutions journalism approaches cannot be generalised along Global North/Global South lines but are instead reshaped within specific political, economic, and structural conditions.

title: Through Rose-Tinted Smart Glasses: Tech Myths and the Normalisation of Wearable Harms
authors: Milica Stilinovic, Joanne E. Gray, Sanika Vekhande, Ben Egliston, Wenqi Tan, Ryan Stanton, Marcus Carter
abstract: Smart glasses are marketed as lifestyle devices that enhance productivity, creativity, and social connection. However, a growing body of evidence suggests these devices are facilitating new harms relating to privacy, bystander consent, and human agency. This paper examines how branded social media content contributes to the normalisation of smart glasses usage while obscuring their associated risks. Focusing on Instagram as a key promotional environment, this study conducts a quantitative content analysis of 768 branded posts featuring Meta’s market leading Ray-Ban glasses alongside emerging competitors Xiaomi, Rokid, Even Realities, and XReal. We analyse how smart-glasses practices are visually and narratively represented and evaluate how recording visibility is addressed and how potential harms are downplayed or obscured. Results suggest that even within highly commercial advertising environments, social and ethical harms remain embedded in the representation of the technology itself. Branded content therefore plays a critical role in legitimising these devices through the construction of powerful technological myths.

title: Linking Media Effects with Political Talk: A Theoretical Review
abstract: Political talk has been a central focus of political communication research. However, grounded in a micro-conversational perspective often fall short in explaining the emergence of diverse forms of political discourse, as well as recent declines in both news use and participation in political talk. By presenting a macro-structural view of political talk and revisiting two classical media effects, this article provides a theoretical review on how agenda-setting and framing effects of general media and mediated communication can shape political talk, across cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions. Theoretically linking media effects with political talk contributes to explaining macro-structural conditions for various political talk to happen, integrates both traditional and non-institutionalized forms of political talk, and generates a set of propositions and research questions to guide future empirical inquiry.

title: Japanese has effectively only two accent patterns: A quantitative and information-theoretic approach to lexical predictability
abstract: Japanese pitch accent is traditionally described as a free accent system allowing up to n + 1 possible patterns for an n-mora word. However, Japanese accentuation is heavily constrained by factors such as word length, prosodic structure, and lexical stratum, leading to the hypothesis that the system fundamentally reduces to only two dominant patterns: unaccented and thematic (antepenultimate). Evaluating this claim requires moving beyond raw counts of empirically attested patterns to quantify the skewness of their distribution. In this study, we introduce information-theoretic metrics, specifically Shannon's conditional entropy and ecological effective numbers of diversity, to measure the uncertainty an diversity of accent patterns in a representative sample of 8,173 Japanese common nouns. Our findings show that while overall pattern richness reaches the theoretical maximum (7 patterns), global effective diversity remains low (3.12 by type frequency, 3.43 by token frequency). Crucially, with knowledge of word length, prosodic structure, and lexical stratum the number of accent patterns is reduced to effectively two (2.1) dominant patterns, providing a precise, quantitative validation of the two-pattern hypothesis. We further demonstrate that prosodic structure is the single most informative factor, reducing accentuation uncertainty by 23%, and that native nouns exhibit greater residual uncertainty than Sino-Japanese and foreign words. Finally, the strong alignment between type and token results confirms that dictionary-based word lists closely mirror natural speech distributions in phonological diversity.

title: Analysis of the effectiveness of the procurement and receipt process of goods in supporting retail store operations
abstract: CV Chiko Mitra Abadi is a retail company in Bandung Regency operating a one-stop shop concept that combines a supermarket, furniture, and playground facilities. Because the company depends on suppliers for all merchandise sold, the effectiveness of its procurement and receipt of goods process is central to maintaining stock availability, data accuracy, and smooth store operations. This report was compiled from Practical Work carried out in the administrative section of CV Chiko Mitra Abadi from June 29 to August 7, 2026, during which the author was directly involved in supplier data management, Purchase Order (PO) preparation, goods receiving, SKU/PLU verification, price and margin updates, and the preparation of promotional media. The report describes the company's procurement and receipt workflow, identifies the operational obstacles encountered during implementation, and evaluates the process using SWOT analysis. The findings show that CV Chiko Mitra Abadi already applies clear procedures supported by formal Purchase Order documentation and generally good coordination among the Administrative, Receiving, warehouse, and supplier-facing functions. However, several weaknesses remain, including administrative tasks that are still performed manually, price and margin updates that are not yet system-integrated, and inspection procedures that slow down when incoming volumes are high, compounded by suppliers' delivery reliability. Based on these findings, the report recommends greater use of integrated information systems, closer and more structured supplier coordination, standardized receiving checklists, and regular employee training, together with a more consumer-centric view of how these administrative improvements ultimately affect customer experience on the sales floor. These recommendations are intended to help the company run its procurement and receiving process more effectively and sustain the smooth operation of its retail store.

title: Agentic AI in Data Commons and GLAM: What Role for the Model Context Protocol?
abstract: The emergence of the agentic web, in which AI agents autonomously navigate online services to accomplish complex tasks, poses urgent questions for digital commons and GLAM institutions (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums). This paper reports on a crosssectoral workshop held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which examined the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new infrastructure layer for regulating agentic access to open knowledge resources. Drawing on presentations by practitioners and researchers across the library, archive, museum, performing arts, open knowledge, and open science sectors, the paper documents emerging MCP experiments, identifies transversal governance challenges, and synthesizes the outcomes of a collective prospective scenario-building exercise. Key findings include: the reframing of MCP server deployment as an editorial act with significant implications for data representation and institutional authority; the identification of critical capacity gaps between API-ready and non-API-ready organizations; and the recognition of MCP governance as a site of broader advocacy for the commons and public goods within the agentic web.

title: Long-term population resilience: an archaeological perspective
abstract: This paper critically examines whether archaeological and palaeoenvironmental research on past population resilience has focused on analytically unsuitable questions and scales. It argues that the nature of the material record constrains the identification of resilient adaptations in the commonsense use of the term, particularly when studies privilege short-lived “pulse” disturbances such as catastrophic events. Instead, the paper advocates greater attention to long-term processes that better align with the temporal granularity of archaeological data. It further interrogates dominant theoretical frameworks derived from complex adaptive systems, highlighting their limited empirical operability, and contrasts them with ecological definitions of resilience grounded in measurable dynamics. The discussion introduces the distinction between resilience and robustness, suggesting that past socio-ecological systems may have favored heterogeneity and non-optimisation to mitigate risk, obviating the need for ‘resilience’ throughout the vast majority of human history. Ultimately, the paper is a call for recalibrating expectations, methods, and narratives to better capture long-term adaptive variability in human history.

title: The Post-Neolithic Anomaly? How ‘Civilisation’ Might Be An Aberration in Human History.
abstract: For the majority of its existence, our species did not live in settlements, did not have agriculture, writing or metallurgy. These are all features of the Holocene Epoch, and the global human population during most of the time since the start of that epoch remained both low and relatively constant until the beginning of the 19th Century, accelerating through the 20th Century, following the Industrial and Agrarian Revolutions. The enormous population, and the complex, planet-wide capitalist technological civilisation on which they depend, but which also exploits them, are now faced with numerous dangers, which are likely to prove insuperable.

title: Unraveling why, how and under which conditions do green interventions improve health and wellbeing in deprived neighborhoods: a realist review
authors: Jonáh Stunt, Jessica C. Kiefte-de Jong, Birthe Jongeneel-Grimen
abstract: Background: Approximately 75% of the European Union population lives in urban areas, a proportion expected to exceed 80% by 2050. Urban green spaces (UGS) are widely recognized for promoting health and well-being. Interventions that increase or improve UGS have been associated with greater use of green spaces and higher levels of physical activity, contributing to positive physical and mental health outcomes. Such interventions may be especially beneficial for lower socioeconomic status (SES) groups living in deprived neighborhoods. However, systematic reviews report inconsistent and sometimes contradictory evidence regarding the positive health effects of UGS interventions in these areas. Without understanding the essential elements and processes underlying effectiveness, it remains unclear why certain interventions succeed and how they can be transferred to other contexts. To address this gap, a realist review was conducted to identify and map the mechanisms and processes through which UGS interventions may improve health in deprived neighborhoods. Methods: An iterative realist review methodology was used to uncover why, how, for whom, and under what conditions UGS interventions are effective. Initial theory development drew on input from residents and professionals, as well as scientific and grey literature. The review followed the RAMESES Quality Standards for Realist Reviews. Retrieved studies were systematically screened and iteratively analyzed to develop Context–Mechanism–Outcome Configurations (CMOCs) and an overarching Realist Programme Theory. Results: Sixteen articles were synthesized, resulting in 17 CMOCs grouped into five themes: social capital, lower thresholds for physical activity, enjoyment of nature, safety, and community involvement. These themes clarify how and under which circumstances UGS interventions can positively influence health in deprived neighborhoods. Key mechanisms include social processes (e.g., increased social support and cohesion), physical processes (e.g., greater physical activity and reduced stress and fatigue), and psychological processes (e.g., mental restoration and improved concentration). Community participation emerged as a cross-cutting mechanism that can activate all pathways by bringing residents together across demographic differences. Environmental, individual, social, and cultural factors shape the extent to which these mechanisms are triggered. Conclusion: UGS interventions operate through multiple, interrelated dynamics. Effective implementation requires attention to diverse (environmental) improvements and to the local mechanisms at play. Tailoring interventions to community needs is essential to ensure that residents of deprived neighborhoods fully benefit from urban green spaces.

title: Municipal Political Representation and Housing Affordability
abstract: Housing affordability has become a pressing issue in many communities, and municipal governments play a critical role in shaping the character and quantity of local housing supply. At present, however, we know little about the extent to which municipal politicians are equipped to represent their constituents’ preferences on housing supply and housing affordability. In this paper, we combine a nationally representative survey of Canadians with a survey of more than 700 mayors and councillors in municipalities across Canada to explore (a) the extent to which politicians align with their constituents in their housing policy attitudes and (b) the extent to which politicians' views are more representative of more privileged local residents, such as homeowners. Across nine concrete housing policy proposals, we find strong evidence of macro-level policy representation: when local communities are more supportive of a housing policy proposals, local politicians tend to be more supportive as well. We also find that politicians' attitudes on housing are not more aligned with privileged local residents; instead, elite-mass alignment is primarily shaped by ideological congruence. These findings suggest that slow progress on housing policy is driven not by policy misalignment between politicians and citizens, but instead by patterns of local mobilization and "neighborhood defender" behavior.

title: Migration as Labor Governance: Empire, Replaceability, and Worker Power
abstract: Why does substantial worker mobilization generate effective leverage in some settings but not in others? This article argues that the answer depends partly on labor governance: the institutions through which labor is recruited, legally differentiated, disciplined, and rendered replaceable. Extending the Empire Theory of Migration (ETM), I distinguish the imperial production of migrant labor from its subsequent organization as labor supply. I develop the argument through three historically connected farmworker campaigns: the National Farm Labor Union’s struggle against the DiGiorgio Fruit Corporation, the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, and the United Farm Workers. Their divergent outcomes—failed recognition, incomplete institutionalization, and contingent bargaining success—show that mobilization generates leverage only when workers and their allies can raise the costs of employer resistance despite employers’ access to alternative labor supplies. Drawing on Ernesto Galarza’s political economy of the Bracero Program, undocumented recruitment, deportation, and labor contracting, the article identifies recruitment, regulation, and legitimation as interconnected dimensions of labor governance. Empire produces migrant labor; labor governance organizes that labor as labor supply; replaceability conditions worker power.

title: A History of Macroeconomics
authors: Francesco Sergi, Beatrice Cherrier, Aurélien Saïdi, Pedro Duarte, Aurélien Goutsmedt, Matthieu Renault, Juan Acosta
abstract: This book offers a history of macroeconomics (the study of “the economy” as a whole) from its inception in the interwar period to today. Its novelty is twofold: it goes beyond a history of theories to cover a wider range of macroeconomists’ practices; it relies on a growing body of historical research, challenging misconceptions commonly disseminated in macroeconomics textbooks. This is not “yet another history of macroeconomics”. It is one that should strike scholars and students in macroeconomics as novel. Such a history is needed because macroeconomics textbooks project a particular “identity” of the field, derived from a specific historical narrative, in which the field evolved through theoretical “revolutions” and “battles” between “schools of thought” initiated by “great men”. We argue that this misrepresents the actual dynamics of macroeconomics. Our history conveys a different perspective, highlighting a more diverse set of characteristics (what macroeconomics is about) and practices (what macroeconomists do). We emphasise how macroeconomics has always relied on the combination of research agendas (theoretical, mathematical, empirical, and computational); how the interaction with other fields (notably microeconomics and econometrics) has been constant; and how the field has been shaped by a cast of researchers with diverse geographical and institutional origins (some working within academia, others in policymaking institutions and private organisations). We bring these many dimensions together through a simple chronology outlining four periods: birth (1920s-1940s), bridges (1950s-1960s), frictions (1970s-1980s), and constellations (1990s-2000s).

title: Moving targets? Life-course dynamics in intergenerational mobility
authors: Roujman Shahbazian, Erik Bihagen, Edvin Syk
abstract: Research on intergenerational mobility assumes that individuals reach occupational maturity, typically around age 35, allowing occupational positions to be treated as stable destinations and mobility to be summarized by a single estimate. We argue that this assumption is difficult to reconcile with contemporary occupational careers. If occupational positions continue to evolve throughout adulthood, intergenerational mobility may itself be a life-course process rather than a fixed parameter. Using retrospective occupational histories from 27 European countries and the United States, we first show that occupational mobility commonly extends well beyond the age conventionally assumed to mark occupational maturity. We then analyze Swedish population register data, estimating parent–offspring associations across every combination of parental and offspring ages between 27 and 56. Rather than converging to a stable value, intergenerational associations vary systematically over the life course, peaking in mid-adulthood before declining. These findings challenge the view that age-related variation primarily reflects measurement error. Instead, they suggest that intergenerational mobility is continuously reshaped by intragenerational mobility over the life course, raising the more fundamental question of whether there exists a single intergenerational mobility parameter to recover.

title: The Stratification Engine: A Recurrent Mechanism of Compound Exclusion
abstract: Resource deprivation cuts two ways. It blocks access to new technologies, and scarcity can narrow the cognitive bandwidth needed to use them. I formalise this as the Resource–Technology–Cognitive (RTC) chain, in which disadvantage compounds at the interfaces between layers, so that exclusion multiplies rather than adds. Cognitive inheritance, reconstituted each generation through early-life conditions rather than genetically transmitted, is posited to carry this compound disadvantage across generations unless those conditions change. I trace the chain across eight technological transitions as an illustrative basis, and derive three falsifiable propositions about sequential causation, super-additive amplification, and intergenerational moderation. The AI transition restructures access and skill demands simultaneously, and the next cohort's starting conditions are already forming.

title: Public Attitudes Toward National Border Controls
abstract: How do citizens evaluate national border controls? In this paper, we argue that while public attitudes toward national border controls are not necessarily fixed, they are primarily interpreted through the lens of migration. To test this argument, we conduct an original survey in Germany and combine open-ended questions with a conjoint and an information experiment. The findings show that migration is not only strongly associated with national border controls, but that the reduction of irregular immigration is also the most important dimension when evaluating these controls. Nonetheless, the findings provide evidence that attitudes toward these controls are not fully fixed: Information on the benefits of the Schengen free travel agreement modestly increases support for border-free travel and reduces support for national border controls. The results have important implications for how the public assesses national border controls in the European context.

title: Exploring the impact of inference method, character coding scheme, and cognacy criterion on phylolinguistic inference: The case of the Japonic language family
authors: Thomas Pellard, Kenan Celik, Reiko Aso, Yosuke Igarashi, Masatoshi Matsunami
abstract: The application of phylogenetic methods to linguistic data requires several critical methodological choices, yet their relative influence on the resulting trees remains poorly understood. This study conducts a systematic sensitivity analysis to evaluate the impact of three key factors: (1) the phylogenetic inference method (neighbor-joining, maximum parsimony, and Bayesian inference), (2) the character coding scheme (binary vs. multistate), and (3) the cognacy (i.e. homology) criterion (root-based vs. stem-based cognacy). Using the Japonic language family as a model, we generated a diverse set of phylogenetic trees and compared them using multiple tree metrics and distance measures between trees. Variance partitioning through distance-based redundancy analysis reveals a clear hierarchy of influence: the choice of inference method is the primary driver of variation between trees, followed by the character coding scheme, while the cognacy criterion exerts a comparatively minor effect. Specifically, we show that the choice of inference method fundamentally shapes tree topology, whereas the character coding scheme impacts branch lengths and evolutionary tempo. While maintaining a consistent and transparent definition of cognacy remains good practice, our results indicate that the choice of one definition over another does not always lead to a significant loss of phylogenetic signal. Therefore, phylolinguistic research should prioritize first and foremost the rigorous selection of inference method.

title: When statistics outlive their geography: asynchronous propagation of a secondary medical area redefinition across Japan's national health data infrastructure — a measurable instance of institutional debt
abstract: Health-system geographies are periodically redefined, but the national statistical products that encode them are updated on independent schedules. We report a natural experiment in how such a redefinition propagates. Effective 1 April 2024, Akita Prefecture consolidated its secondary medical areas (SMAs) from eight to three — the only SMA reorganization under Japan’s 8th Medical Plan cycle — reducing the national SMA count from 335 to 330. We examined how three national data products required for SMA-level analysis of the same reference year (2024) encoded the change, by comparing their SMA code sets and validating municipal re-aggregations against published totals. The Physician, Dentist and Pharmacist Statistics 2024 (census date 31 December 2024; released December 2025) and the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare’s municipality–SMA correspondence table (version dated April 2026) encode the new three-SMA definition. The 11th NDB Open Data, released June 2026, tabulates fiscal-year 2024 claims — all generated after the redefinition took effect — in the superseded eight-SMA geography. No product declares the vintage of its zone definition as metadata; the divergence surfaces only as unexplained code mismatches — and, for three zone codes reused across definitions, as silent mis-joins — observable from published artifacts alone. We interpret this as a measurable instance of institutional debt — the divergence between legally effective definitions and those encoded in infrastructure, with reconciliation labor externalized to analysts — quantifiable along three axes (lag, affected population, repairability). Contrasting England’s centrally remapped response to its 2022 commissioning-geography transition, we propose that zone-level statistics be published as versioned views over stable unit identifiers with mandatory definition-vintage metadata.

title: Geodemographic Inequalities in Battery Electric Vehicle Adoption across UK Neighbourhoods
authors: Alex Singleton, Ian Philips, Jillian Anable
abstract: Battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption is an important contributor to the decarbonisation of road transport in the UK and other OECD countries, yet uptake remains highly uneven between places. This paper examines the geography of privately kept battery electric vehicles across UK small areas using quarterly DVLA vehicle licensing records, linked geodemographically to the 2021/22 UK Output Area Classification. The analysis measures observed private vehicle ownership at neighbourhood scale, enabling within local authority variation to be examined directly. The results show that BEV penetration is strongly right-skewed, with adoption concentrated in affluent professional neighbourhoods, prosperous suburban and rural areas, and dense urban cores with relatively small but rapidly electrifying private fleets. Lower uptake is associated with neighbourhoods characterised by rented tenure, terraced housing and flats, where access to private off-street charging is likely to be more constrained. Partitioning the national time series by geodemographic type reveals that the aggregate adoption curve is composed of distinct trajectories, with some early-adopting neighbourhood types showing signs of slower recent growth while later-adopting groups continue to accelerate. Residuals from the geodemographic baseline are spatially clustered, indicating that neighbourhood composition alone does not explain the geography of adoption. The paper demonstrates the value of combining administrative vehicle records with geodemographic classification to identify where BEV adoption is leading, lagging and diverging from demographic expectation, with implications for a more equitable rollout of charging infrastructure and transport decarbonisation policy.

title: Cultures of Civil Crisis Preparedness
abstract: Recent crises, including pandemics, extreme weather events, and humanitarian crises, have demonstrated informal civil society’s role as a crucial first responder to crisis situations. Yet crisis management research and policy have largely treated informal civil society as a spontaneous resource activated only during response and recovery and lack a conceptual understanding of informal civil society in the crisis preparation phase. This article develops a theoretical framework for understanding cultures of civil crisis preparedness: shared repertoires of perceived responsibilities and preparedness strategies through which civil society anticipates and prepares for future crises. The framework specifies how a community's crisis perceptions shape both responsibilities and strategies, how trust networks enable mutual coordination, and how institutional crisis management approaches, geographical exposure, and authorities' crisis communication shape informal civil society's role in preparedness. It thereby enables analysis of how people come to imagine their own and others' responsibilities before crises occur, and why cultures of civil crisis preparedness vary across national and local contexts.

title: Prospective Travel Diary in Tourist Decision-Making
abstract: This research note introduces a new image-based tool that integrates inspiration and co-creation in tourist decision-making. Grounded in prospective memory – a concept developed in psychology literature- the tool enables participants to mentally simulate and visualize a future trip, constructing a fictitious travel diary through illustrated cards. This approach serves as both a research method for studying decision-making processes and a practical tool for tourism professionals. We explore its theoretical foundations, applications, and potential to enhance tourist engagement and travel booking experiences.

title: Deliberative, affective, and experiential risk in crisis response: Fears of responders and people in crisis
authors: Andrew David Eaton, Megan Wheeler Rowe, Claire Ryder, Amanda Mathew, Sandra Kwan, Jenny Hui, Brandon Barksdale, Leyna Lowe
abstract: Mental health crisis response is diverse and evolving, with ongoing debate about outcomes for people in crisis, the appropriateness of different responses, and the role of police. Crisis encounters combine three forms of risk assessment: reasoned judgments (deliberative), emotional responses (affective), and gut feelings (experiential). This qualitative knowledge-to-action study consisted of interviews with 33 Canadian and American key informants in crisis response (e.g., responders and people with lived experience of crisis encounters). Interpretive phenomenological analysis was employed by a large and diverse coding team on data pertaining to shifting dynamics and experiences of risk. Findings address: a) the governing logic of risk in crisis response, as risks are triaged and translated yet remain subjective and uncertain; b) constant perceptions of risk in crisis encounters that shift based on the scene and mental health discourses; and c) a double-bind to police involvement, where responders fear risks to themselves and others on scene and seek security and stability in police but people in crisis fear police involvement. Risk moves from deliberative to experiential via affective emotions on the scene. This study identified sustained reliance on police by responders, even within civilian-led, non-police alternative crisis response teams. Police remain a form of first response, co-response, and backup or escalation support, heightening risk for people in crisis, despite focused efforts to de-task police from crisis calls.

title: Backcasting Semantic Risk Indicators in Historical Travel Advisories: Enriching a Longitudinal Web Corpus
abstract: Travel warnings can affect the political and economic situation in the target countries. However, data to systematically investigate these links are lacking. Previous work has introduced and validated a crawler pipeline to obtain time series of government-issued travel advisories via the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine. Governments may change the type and amount of information they provide in their advisories. For example, the United States began to provide numerical travel warning levels for individual countries and tags to categorize advisories in 2018. We illustrate an approach to using these \textit{labeled} data points to extend the variable for travel advisories before 2018 and for other issuing countries. In addition, we show how to extract additional information, such as whether the advisory concerns an entire country or specific regions or cities. This paper documents a further step towards a harmonized and unified dataset and a multilingual text corpus of government-issued travel advisories for the social sciences, humanities, and beyond.

title: Population Development In The Roman Empire
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing the population development of the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire despite the scarcity, inconsistency, and indirect nature of the available evidence. Its primary objective is to produce a continuous population curve spanning from 508 BC to AD 395, which is internally consistent in the assumptions of underlying growth and other factors over time. To achieve this, the study critically integrates multiple methodological approaches, including Beloch’s area-and-density estimates, Lo Cascio’s revisions, and Scheidel’s demographic critiques, alongside archaeological, economic, and comparative demographic evidence. By combining these methods and cross-validating their results, a coherent framework is established for estimating both population levels and growth rates. It adopts moderate empire-wide growth assumptions, 2-3‰ annually, while allowing for significant variation between core and newly incorporated territories. This enables the interpolation between key chronological benchmarks and the extension of estimates across periods lacking direct evidence. The resulting reconstruction yields a continuous demographic trajectory showing the full consequences of the growth assumptions.

title: Ready for What? Rethinking AI and Robotics Preparedness for Adoption and Policy
abstract: Efforts to accelerate AI and robotics adoption require evidence about where communities are prepared to act and where support is still needed. However, conclusions based mainly on average differences between people or stakeholder groups can obscure relationships that emerge when the same person evaluates different challenges. We address this problem using a repeated card-based survey in which 982 participants provided 15,200 evaluations of 17 AI and robotics challenges. Each challenge was rated on common 1-5 measures of significance, complexity and readiness, where readiness refers to perceived community preparedness and available resources rather than personal competence or realised adoption. Because each participant evaluated multiple challenges, the design separates stable differences between respondents from challenge-specific deviations within the same respondent. This distinction materially changes the interpretation of preparedness. Within the same respondent, a challenge rated one point more complex than their usual level is associated with approximately 0.21 points lower readiness ($p<0.001$). By contrast, respondents who generally rate challenges as more complex do not systematically report lower readiness ($p=0.29$). Significance is positively associated with readiness, while unusually high complexity modestly weakens this challenge-specific alignment. These relationships also vary strongly across challenge families, and professional background remains associated with adjusted preparedness assessments. On applied cards, confidence, trust and related perceptions provide substantial additional information about readiness, including for held-out participants. For policymakers and organisations, the findings show that averaging across stakeholders can hide challenge-specific barriers. Readiness assessments should therefore preserve both differences between stakeholder groups and variation within the same stakeholders across challenges. Effective adoption and literacy strategies should ask not only \emph{who} appears ready, but \emph{which challenges} they find unusually difficult and whether the likely constraint concerns implementation, capability, assurance or resources.

title: Technological complexity and the nature of adaptive problem-solving in small-scale societies
authors: Marcus J. Hamilton, Briggs Buchanan, Robert S. Walker, Mark Collard, Nicholas Gala
abstract: Technological complexity is a defining eature of human adaptation, yet the processes determining how much technology societies require remain poorly understood. Existing explanations emphasize environmental risk, resource productivity, or demographic factors, but provide limited insight into why technological systems respond differently across subsistence economies. Here, we propose that technological complexity reflects the computational burden imposed by environmental uncertainty. In seasonal environments, survival requires solving a sequential decision problem in which risks accumulate multiplicatively across the year, increasing demand for technological buffering. Technologies reduce this uncertainty but are costly to produce and maintain, generating an optimization problem balancing risk reduction against technological costs. We further argue that niche construction fundamentally alters this relationship by smoothing environmental variability and transforming exogenous uncertainty into managed, endogenous processes. From this framework we derive the prediction that technological complexity should increase with environmental seasonality among hunter-gatherers but become increasingly independent of climate as niche construction intensifies. We test these predictions using data on toolkit richness and component-part diversity from 127 small-scale societies. We find the richness of hunter-gatherer technologies increases exponentially with environmental seasonality, whereas farming technologies remain largely invariant across climatic regimes. These findings suggest that technological complexity responds to the informational and computational demands environmental conditions impose. More broadly, these results imply that agriculture represents not simply a new mode of energy acquisition, but a transition in the computational architecture of human adaptation, in which farming reduces the effective depth of adaptive problems by restructuring the environments that generate uncertainty.
