title: 从宗教圣地到茶道名片——汉口亚历山大·涅夫斯基教堂的百年变迁 From Sacred Sanctuary to Tea Trade Landmark: The Century-Long Transformation of the Hankou Alexander Nevsky Church
abstract: 本文以武汉现存唯一的东正教建筑——汉口阿列克桑德聂夫堂（亚历山大·涅夫斯基教堂）为研究对象，系统梳理了其自1876年草创、历经晚清“东方茶港”繁荣、民国常态化发展直至建国后高度式微的百年历史变迁。文章结合实地考察，深入探讨了该建筑在2013年依托中俄“万里茶道”地缘历史叙事重获抢救性修缮的风貌复原过程。同时，作者指出，在当下的世俗化利用与展览叙事中，当局呈现出一种既渴望吸纳历史建筑的外交红利、又刻意回避其本源宗教属性与制度化衰落历史的矛盾心态。本研究不仅丰富了近代通商口岸异质信仰群体的微观历史，也为审视当代历史遗产保护中的意识形态焦虑与话语置换提供了参考。 Taking the Alexander Nevsky Church, the only surviving Orthodox architectural heritage in Wuhan, as the research object, this paper systematically delineates its century-long historical evolution, tracing its origins in 1876, its flourishing period during the late Qing Dynasty when Hankou served as the "Oriental Tea Port," its regularized development during the Republican era, and its post-1949 institutional decline. Based on field observations, the study examines the facade restoration process initiated in 2013, which was driven by the geopolitical and historical narrative of the Sino-Russian "Great Tea Road." Furthermore, the author points out a nuanced paradox in the contemporary secular utilization and exhibition narratives of the property: the authorities eagerly embrace the diplomatic dividends and cultural prestige of the historic building, while deliberately avoiding its fundamental religious attributes and the complex history of its institutional decline. This study not only enriches the microhistory of heterogeneous religious groups in modern treaty ports, but also provides empirical insights into ideological anxieties and discourse displacement in contemporary historical heritage conservation.

title: Great Expectations? Researchers in Germany are Optimistic about the Potential of Grant Lotteries.
abstract: In this study I investigate researchers’ expectations towards the potential advantages of grant lotteries in a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions provided by the Scientists Survey of the German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies (DZHW). I describe the saliency of the two debates on bias in grant peer review and on grant lotteries, as well as researchers’ levels of experience with grant peer review. I use both descriptive statistics and analytical models to investigate which characteristics shape scientists’ relative grant lottery optimism. I find that experienced and more senior scientists are significantly less optimistic about grant lotteries. Saliency and reviewer workload are positively associated with optimism. I conclude that, even though saliency of the issue remains sparse, researchers are generally optimistic about grant lotteries, yet also aware of some of their potential disadvantages.

title: Individual perception of bias in grant peer review strongly associated with openness towards the introduction of lotteries.
abstract: This study of a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions investigates researchers’ individual perception of bias in grant peer review and their openness towards the potential introduction of grant lotteries, as well as the potential link between the two concepts. Indeed, bias in peer review is often cited in the theoretical debate on grant lotteries. But even though researchers are both very involved in and strongly affected by grant decision-making, there is not enough empirical evidence on their perspective. I find that bias perception is very prevalent, openness is generally rare and researchers who perceive more bias in grant peer review are more open towards grant lotteries in a substantial and statistically significant way.

title: Domestic Peace Deficit: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Gender-Based Violence through Institutional, Relational, and Structural Peace Failures
abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) continues to persist at high levels despite decades of legal reform, policy intervention, and scholarly attention. Existing approaches, drawn from criminology, public health, sociology, psychology, and law, have generated important insights into individual acts, risk factors, and immediate responses. Yet they remain less equipped to explain the cumulative institutional conditions that allow harm within domestic and intimate life to endure across the life course. This paper introduces the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) as a conceptual framework that addresses this gap. DPD explains how cumulative institutional failures undermine peace within domestic life by shaping exposure to violence, access to protection, and recognition of harm. Its central contribution is to treat the household as a peace system rather than merely a private social space or a site of interpersonal violence. Drawing on and extending insights from structural violence, positive peace, feminist peace research, human security, the ecological model of GBV, and intersectionality, the framework organises analysis around three pillars: the Violence and Coercion Deficit, the Agency and Relational Peace Deficit, and the Institutional and Structural Support Deficit. The paper defines domestic peace, formalises the deficit concept, outlines core principles, describes how the framework was developed, sketches pathways of accumulation, a future measurement agenda, and states the framework's principal limitations. DPD does not replace existing theories; it integrates and extends them into a coherent architecture centred on the domestic sphere. In doing so, it offers researchers, policymakers, and practitioners a tool for understanding why formal protections so often fail to produce lived safety, and for designing responses that address institutional recognition, accountability, and the intergenerational transmission of harm.

title: Identity Claims in Political Speech
authors: Asli Ceren Cinar, Mirya Holman, Tyler Simko
abstract: Social identities shape political behavior, but when, how, and why do people talk about these identities? We introduce the concept of identity claiming: publicly identifying oneself as a member of a social group to establish standing and strengthen political appeals. Drawing on five corpora of political communication, including congressional newsletters, campaign biographies, social media, and public comments at school board and city council meetings, we show that elites and members of the public regularly make identity claims. The identities they invoke are not random: claims match the setting, deserving reference groups are used more frequently, and identity claims associated with increased vocal pitch. Experimental and social media evidence shows that speech with identity claims prompts engagement from the audience. Our work shows how ordinary people and political elites strategically and frequently engage in identity politics in their public communication.

title: Das gelesene Buch. Lesen und Geschmackspräferenzen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz
authors: Carolin Amlinger, Luca Keiser, Oliver Nachtwey, Jörg Rössel
abstract: This preprint presents descriptive findings from a standardised online survey on book reading conducted in Germany, Austria and Switzerland in May and June 2026 (N = 6,427; quota-sampled by gender, age, region and education). It asks how reading practices and literary preferences are socially distributed across the German-speaking countries. The findings suggest that what divides the reading public is not how much is read but whether people read at all: the share of avid readers varies only between 5 and 13 per cent across social groups, whereas the share of non-readers ranges from 7 to 30 per cent. Education marks the sharpest boundary, with the decisive break falling between the highly educated and everyone else rather than along a continuous gradient. Gender and having been read to in childhood operate as independent axes, while age structures taste more than volume. Evaluative criteria follow the same logic: immersion and involvement dominate across all groups, but formal criteria such as stylistic quality and complexity gain weight with education. At the same time, the cultural legitimacy of the book remains broadly acknowledged, including among those who barely read. The analysis is deliberately descriptive and serves as a first step towards subsequent multivariate analyses of the social and literary space.

title: Support and contestation under the radar: How states promote and undermine the international fight against corruption
abstract: This article investigates hidden forms of support for and contestation of international norms. Existing research largely focuses on publicly visible behavioural forms of contestation, such as member states’ exit from international organizations (IOs). However, less visible practices can also effectively undermine and sabotage international norms, or, conversely, strengthen them. We explore this phenomenon by researching a prominent IO in the global fight against corruption, the Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), by means of interviews with delegates to GRECO and members of the Council of Europe secretariat, complemented with an analysis of policy documents. The empirical evidence reveals five distinct types of hidden contestation and two types of hidden support. Contestation typically originates from the political macro-level rather than from the involved expert community. Member states contest GRECO’s authority through ineffective implementation, delays, obstructive voting, and by negotiating review outcomes. Conversely, peer pressure and peer support emerge as meaningful micro-level practices of norm support that counteract contestation. This study’s insights advance research on contestation and support of international norms and inform research, theory, and practice on how to strengthen the global fight against corruption.

title: A Healthier Start Abroad? The health at birth of the children of migrants and of those born at origin
abstract: The health of migrants is mostly studied in relation to destination-country natives, Origin-country comparisons are rarely pursued, even though they provide a more convincing counterfactual, allowing us to (a) measure “health gains” from migration, (b) disentangle mechanisms including selectivity, cultural factors and contextual change, (c) elucidate the relationship between migration and global health inequality. We address this gap by comparing the health at birth of children born in Spain to migrant parents from 15 origin countries with that of children born in those same origin countries, using Spanish vital statistics linked to Demographic and Health Surveys and other origin-country sources. We find that, for most groups, the children of migrants are healthier at birth (measured via low birth weight) than children in their parents' origin countries. This is also true among groups disadvantaged relative to Spanish natives, and is more pronounced for non-Western and, especially, Asian-origin groups. We find limited support for cultural explanations and stronger support for both migrant selectivity and improved contextual conditions at destination. Though the latter two are not fully separable, our evidence favors the effect of the change in contextual conditions. These results suggest migration can function as an equalizing force, narrowing birthplace-based health inequalities.

title: When Resources Are Scarce: Formal Mentoring as a Compensatory Resource for Sustainable Performance Expectations
abstract: Drawing on Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, this study conceptualizes formal mentoring as a resource system and examines how mentoring functions, job resources and demands, self-empowerment, and organizational support relate to mentoring program effectiveness and sustainable performance expectations. Using cross-sectional self-report data from 71 participants in a formal peer mentoring program, we found that perceived program effectiveness was positively associated with sustainable performance expectations, defined as participants’ beliefs about their ability to sustain performance and well-being over time. Mentoring functions were positively related to program effectiveness and, indirectly, to sustainable performance expectations via perceived mentoring effectiveness. In addition, job cognitive resources, self-empowerment, and organizational support moderated the relationship between mentoring functions and program effectiveness, such that mentoring functions were most strongly associated with perceived effectiveness when these resources were lower. These findings suggest that mentoring functions may operate as compensatory resources in resource-constrained contexts. Employment status was also relevant, with full-time employed participants reporting higher program effectiveness than solopreneurs. Overall, the findings extend JD-R theory by positioning mentoring not only as a developmental intervention but also as a resource that supports sustainable human performance.

title: Standardising Access to Digital Platform Data: A Taxonomy for Social Research
authors: Futoon Abushaqra, Damiano Spina, Amanda Lawrence, Daniel Angus, Robert Glasgow
abstract: [This manuscript has been submitted for peer review] Abstract: Recent regulations granting individuals the right to access their personal data stored on digital platforms have reshaped the landscape of data collection. Under frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union and the 2019 New York SHIELD Act, platforms are now required to provide users with mechanisms to retrieve and inspect their own data; commonly referred to as Data Download Packages (DDPs). These developments have enabled new forms of data collection through data donation, where users voluntarily share their DDPs for research purposes. However, the structure, format, and granularity of DDPs vary significantly across platforms and over time, posing challenges for researchers, especially those without technical expertise. Responding to these challenges, this paper contributes to the Australian Internet Observatory's broader agenda of building national research infrastructure for independent, public-interest platform research. We propose a taxonomy for categorising DDPs across different platforms, alongside a schema repository that systematically describes the content of each DDP, including its structure, data types, and formats. These contributions support a more consistent and comprehensive understanding of DDPs across diverse platforms, with a particular focus on social media and digital services, and enable their effective use in both academic and applied research contexts.

title: Tracking Change, Informing Policy: Longitudinal Evidence of Shifting Political Affiliations and Public Attitudes Toward Higher Education
authors: Stephen M Gavazzi, Suzanne Bartle-Haring, E. Gordon Gee
abstract: This longitudinal study examines how public attitudes toward U.S. public higher education shifted between 2021 and 2025 across five policy-relevant domains: funding priorities, rural-urban engagement, global-local emphasis, financial aid preferences, and the perceived importance of national rankings. Using data from panel respondents across nine states, results show growing support for balanced approaches to geographic engagement, financial aid, and global-local activities, alongside increased prioritization of teaching and declining support for community engagement. Nearly 30 percent of participants changed their political affiliation over the four year period, and these shifts were strongly associated with changes in funding preferences, especially allocations to teaching. Cross lag analyses further indicate that changes in funding priorities, engagement emphases, and ideological self-placement help explain trust in state universities. Findings underscore the importance of longitudinal designs for understanding how individual-level political dynamics shape public expectations for, and confidence in, higher education.

title: New alternatives, same orders: modern alternative proteins did not replace meat purchases in restaurants
authors: Jared Winslow, Jacob Robert Peacock, Jayisha Dhargawe, Hailey Sherman, Seth Ariel Green, Maya Mathur
abstract: Plant-based alternative proteins are widely expected to displace meat consumption and, in turn, reorient the global food system away from the externalities of animal agriculture, but little empirical work has assessed these presumed substitution effects in naturalistic settings. Here, we use a dataset of 1.2 million transactions across seven restaurants and eight years to investigate whether introducing modern alternative proteins to restaurant menus reduces purchases of meat-containing dishes. We analyzed effects on total meat purchases and on category-matched purchases, pairing each alternative protein with the meat it emulates; we also estimate individual (within-customer) purchasing changes. Our results from 40 preregistered outcome-exposure pairings are overwhelmingly null, whether pooled across restaurants or stratified by restaurant. These findings challenge the widespread belief that alternative proteins displace meat purchases.

title: Digital state capacity: a conceptualization approach
abstract: Digital technologies matter more and more for state affairs, yet few formulations define what digital is for the continuous structure of the state after decades of digitalization. This article argues that digital has become an essential dimension of state capacity. Drawing on an ontological-semantic approach to concept building, it constructs the concept of digital capacity around three necessary dimensions: digital apparatus, digital space control and digital interaction. It then develops the Digital Capacity Index, covering the 193 United Nations members from 2001 to 2022. Validity tests show a consistent concept-measure relationship and support comparative policy analysis of the digital state.

title: Two Cycles, Not One: A Continuous-Time Point-Process Analysis of Reciprocal Violence in the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict
abstract: Whether violence in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict is reciprocal — each side's lethal action provoking the other's — has been studied largely through vector-autoregression on time-binned counts, an approach that obscures the timing, branching structure, and directionality of response. We model lethal violence in the two directions as a bivariate Hawkes process, a continuous-time self- and mutually-exciting point process, using individual-incident fatality records from the Second Intifada through October 2023. Reciprocal excitation is genuine but profoundly asymmetric: a single Palestinian-to-Israeli event triggers on the order of one subsequent Israeli lethal event, nearly thirty times the reverse coupling. The asymmetry survives placebo, regime-detection, and flexible-baseline checks designed to rule out a common-driver confound, and goodness-of-fit testing confirms the models describe the data adequately. Allowing the couplings to take either sign, we find no evidence of deterrence in either direction. The strength of the Israeli response is statistically indistinguishable across the conflict's two main eras, but its speed is not: the characteristic response lag roughly halves between the Intifada and the later Gaza-war period, a temporal change binned methods cannot represent. Resolving the Israeli-to-Palestinian direction into its Gaza and West Bank theaters reveals that they operate as nearly independent systems: violence within each is strongly self-exciting while cross-theater coupling is negligible, and the reciprocal dynamic that dominates the pooled analysis is localized almost entirely to the West Bank, whereas Gaza's violence is driven by internal escalation. What appears in aggregate as a single cycle is, spatially, two barely-interacting logics — a separation we argue reflects the differential governance of the two territories rather than any natural division of the conflict. A three-stream extension shows settler violence to be a distinct channel: reactive to Palestinian action, increasingly self-exciting, and temporally preceding rather than following state violence. All findings replicate on an independently constructed event dataset. We document these regularities for 2000–2023 and set out why we do not extend them through the subsequent war: individual-incident records for that period exist, but not on a footing commensurable with the present analysis.

title: The reach of violence: Infant health among diasporas in the United States during the onset of the 2023 Gaza War
authors: Jasmin Abdel Ghany, Emma Romell, Joshua Wilde
abstract: A large body of research documents the harm that armed conflict inflicts on the health of populations in conflict zones. Yet if violence injures collectivities rather than only those who experience it directly, its health consequences should extend to those who identify with affected populations wherever they reside. We test this hypothesis by examining the effects of the October 7, 2023, attacks in Israel and the ensuing onset of the Gaza War on infant health in the United States among mothers born in Israel, the West Bank, and neighboring, Arab, and Muslim-majority countries. In a novel application of the event-study design, we trace month-by-month changes in preterm birth and low birthweight – outcomes that shape health and socioeconomic attainment throughout the life course. Our analyses show that the Israel-born diaspora experienced an immediate, short-lived reversal in their previously substantial infant health advantage after the October 7 attacks. Infant health also deteriorated among mothers born in neighboring, other Arab, and other Muslim-majority countries. These findings indicate that the health consequences of violence are not confined to the conflict zone but extend to geographically distant diaspora communities who are connected to the affected populations by shared national and ethnic origin and religion.

title: Rethinking Social Sustainability Metrics in Chile’s Lithium Sociotechnical Transition: Numbers, Policies and Knowledge
authors: Sebastián Herrera-León, Iván Ojeda-Pereira, Fernando Campos-Medina, Rodrigo Molina-Richardson
abstract: Social sustainability indicators are central decision-support tools in mining, used to evaluate social performance and guide policy and investment. However, these indicators do not merely describe reality; they actively shape it by defining what is measured, reported, and governed. In the context of lithium extraction from brines, this performative role becomes particularly relevant as expanding production and technological changes reconfigure water use, territorial relations, and community livelihoods in sensitive ecosystems such as the high-Andean salt flats of Chile, which host some of the world's largest lithium reserves and production sites. This paper analyses how social sustainability is currently measured in the lithium industry and identifies the opportunities and limitations of existing indicator frameworks. Using a systematic analysis of sustainability reports and international reporting standards, combined with insights from stakeholder interviews, we examine the indicators commonly used to assess lithium extraction activities. The results show that existing indicator systems are structured by global reporting standards and compliance-oriented metrics, whilst territorial dynamics and relational aspects of social sustainability remain partially captured. Based on these results, the paper discusses implications for the design of social sustainability indicators in critical mineral extraction. We argue that improving sustainability assessment requires incorporating territorially situated perspectives, ecosystem-based knowledge, and broader participation of communities, universities, public institutions, and firms. In this sense, redesigning sustainability indicators as more reflexive and participatory tools may support more socially robust pathways in the sociotechnical transition of the lithium industry in Chile.

title: Capitalizing on Controversy: Humor, Scandal Entrepreneurship, and the Rise of the Far Right
abstract: Right-wing public figures, from comedians to politicians, increasingly use humor strategically to provoke scandal. While scandals are typically understood to damage the reputations of norm transgressors, the rise of successful right-wing scandal makers challenges this assumption. In this article, we introduce the concept of ‘scandal entrepreneur’ to theorize the rise of celebrity figures who deliberately create or amplify scandals for personal or political gain. Integrating insights from political scandal research, sociological work on cultural and moral entrepreneurship, and critical humor studies, we develop an innovative approach to scandal that combines dramaturgical and conjunctural analysis. Drawing on a quantitative mapping of Dutch humor scandals between 1990 and 2024 and an in-depth qualitative analysis of two cases, we trace both the steep rise in humor scandals in the early twenty-first century and the increasing professionalization of scandal entrepreneurship, which has turned scandal-making into a profitable business model. Based on our analysis of the Nekschot cartoon scandal (2008) and the VI-Akwasi scandal (2020), we demonstrate that, within the current cultural conjuncture, right-wing actors are best positioned to capitalize on scandals and successfully dramatize social and cultural divides through humor. Our approach offers valuable analytical tools for humor and scandal scholarship and the field of right-wing studies, providing a critical lens through which to examine wider cultural changes.

title: AI Parasocial Relationships and The Potential Role of Miswanting in Loneliness and Emotional Distress: A Theoretical Review
abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence has led to the development of more advanced AI systems that can create human like conversation. This increases the usage of AI chatbots into sources of social interaction, emotional support, and companionship. Recent researches have examined their potential benefits and risk but less attention has been given to the individuals expectations regarding the emotional benefits of artificial intelligence. The present theoretical review proposes miswanting as a central theme for understanding the discrepancy between anticipated and actual emotional fulfilment in human- AI relationship. Drawing upon the theories of miswanting, parasocial relationship, self-determination and loneliness theories this review highlights the conceptual framework linking pre-existing loneliness and unmet emotional needs to AI companion use, emotional attachment, expectations of fulfilment, and subsequent psychological outcomes. The framework proposes that individuals may initially experience AI companionship as emotionally comforting and socially supportive and develops expectations that such interaction can satisfy long term emotional and relatedness needs. When experienced outcomes don’t match with these expectations, an expectation- reality discrepancy occurs which may eventually lead to persistent loneliness, emotional. Importantly, the framework does not assume that AI companionship is inherently harmful; rather, it highlights the potential importance of miswanting theory to the emerging context of AI companionship. This review offers a novel conceptual perspective and generates testable propositions for future empirical research.

title: "It's Just About Being with My Friends": Children's Perspectives on the Use, Risks and Benefits of Virtual Worlds Platforms
abstract: Despite the central role that virtual worlds based on user-generated content, such as Roblox, play in the digital lives of children and adolescents, research incorporating their first-hand experiences and perspectives of these platforms remains limited. Roblox is one of the world's largest virtual world platforms, used predominantly by children and adolescents, with most users estimated to be under the age of 16. Grounded in a children's rights perspective, this study adopts an arts-based qualitative approach that combines cognitive mapping through drawing with follow-up interviews to explore what children's and adolescents' perceptions of Roblox reveal about its risks and benefits. To address this aim, we engaged 29 children aged 10–16 in partnership with an international school in Italy. Our analysis identifies three key findings with theoretical and regulatory implications. First, rather than simply as a game, participants perceive and use Roblox primarily as a social platform where they play and communicate with friends, form new relationships, and maintain long-distance connections. Related to that, participants also perceive Roblox as operating in ways that resemble social media platforms. Second, these social dynamics are closely intertwined with risks, including exposure to scams, toxic interactions, grooming, online dating practices, and monetisation pressures. Third, participants routinely migrate to platforms such as Discord and WhatsApp for communication, circumventing Roblox's age-based restrictions and complicating platform-specific safeguarding efforts. These findings highlight the need for adaptive safeguarding strategies and contribute to theoretical discussions of the increasingly blurred boundaries between digital games and social media and children’s online safety.

title: Ambient Load and Human Dignity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Structural Stability Science (SSS) Briefing on Boundary, Load Displacement, and Institutional Responsibility
abstract: This public-facing institutional briefing applies Structural Stability Science (SSS), Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT), the Structural Identification Method (SIM), and Load–Capacity–Boundary Mechanics (LCB) to a structural question raised by artificial intelligence and human dignity: when machine-mediated systems become more powerful, efficient, opaque, and difficult to contest, where does the Load go? The briefing identifies Ambient Load as non-decomposed Load remaining active as unresolved background demand under conditions of ambiguity, avoidance, unclear authority, unstable Boundary mediation, undefined terms, machine-mediated misclassification, or unlocated responsibility. It further identifies Load Displacement Through Ambiguity as a structural condition in which unresolved ambiguity transfers the burden of clarification, stabilization, correction, compliance, repair, or source preservation onto another actor or system layer. In the institutional context opened by Pope Leo XIV’s public teaching on artificial intelligence and the safeguarding of the human person, this briefing analyzes the convergence between a public moral-institutional concern and a structural-scientific classification problem. It does not provide legal, clinical, theological, compliance, technical AI, or engineering advice and does not authorize use of SSS, DHFT, SIM, LCB, Ambient Load, Structural Drift, or related source architecture for assessment, audit, certification, training, institutional deployment, machine use, implementation, or derivative method development. Technical Note: This record is a public-facing Structural Stability Science briefing. It applies the SSS / DHFT / SIM / LCB source architecture to an institutional question concerning artificial intelligence, human dignity, Ambient Load, Boundary degradation, Load coupling, and Load displacement. It does not replace, modify, or expand the DHFT source architecture and does not authorize assessment, audit, certification, training, implementation, machine use, or derivative method development. title: Assessment of Broadcast Regulation Patterns in Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Hussain Bin Hyacinth, Prof. Abigail Odozi Ogwezzy-Ndisika, Olunifesi Adekunle Suraj
abstract: This paper examined the major patterns of broadcast regulation in Nigeria, their operational dynamics and implications for professionalism, accountability and broadcast media freedom. Through the lens of Social Responsibility Theory, the paper conceptualised broadcast regulation as a multi-layered system comprising self-regulation, internal regulation, statutory regulation and co-regulation. A qualitative case study design was adopted, with data generated through semi-structured interviews involving 15 purposively selected broadcast experts and scholars. The data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings showed that broadcast regulation in Nigeria operates through a combination of individual professional responsibility, organisational control mechanisms, statutory oversight by the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC) and stakeholder participation in regulatory processes. The paper further found that licensing procedures, compliance with Nigeria Broadcasting Code, consultations and enforcement constitute the major operational frameworks of regulation. However, political interference, selective enforcement and the limited autonomy of the NBC emerged as significant challenges. While the regulatory system contributes to professionalism and accountability, concerns regarding ownership influence, regulatory bias and excessive government involvement were found to undermine broadcast media freedom and audience confidence in the regulatory process. The paper concluded that effective broadcast regulation in the country requires a balanced integration of self-regulation, internal regulation, statutory regulation and co-regulation. It, therefore, recommended strengthening the institutional independence of the NBC to ensure fair, transparent and credible regulation capable of promoting both professional standards and broadcast media freedom.

title: Mass Media Agenda Setting Role and the Fight against Crude Oil Theft in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Beatrice Okatubo Manasseh, Ezekiel S. Asemah
abstract: This study examined how the mass media can contribute to efforts aimed at curtailing crude oil theft in Bayelsa State. The paper was anchored on the agenda setting theory as its theoretical framework, while library research method was adopted as its methodology. The paper discovered that the role of the media in curbing crude oil theft is connected to their functions of informing, educating and entertaining society. The paper concluded that the media can assist in combating crude oil theft by giving prominence to the issue and portraying its negative impact on Nigeria, the state, actors and communities. It recommended that the media, especially, radio should increase the amount of time given to the coverage of crude oil theft.

title: Influencers Credibility and Consumer Purchase Decision across Cultures
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Victoria Ukwuamedua, Faith Ozikor Amah
abstract: This study examined the influence of influencer credibility on consumer purchase decisions across cultures. It looked at how trustworthiness, expertise, authenticity and relatability of social media influencers shape consumers’ willingness to accept product recommendations and make purchase decisions in different cultural contexts. The study is based on the source credibility theory. The study adopts a library research methodology, drawing on existing scholarly works, textbooks and journal articles on influencer marketing, consumer behaviour and cross-cultural communication. Findings from the reviewed literature show that influencer credibility plays a significant role in shaping consumer trust and purchase intentions. However, its influence varies across cultures due to differences in values, communication styles and perceptions of authenticity. In some cultural settings, consumers prioritise expertise and professionalism, while in others, relatability and lifestyle similarity are more important. The study further reveals that although credible influencers can increase consumer engagement and purchase intention, other factors such as cultural orientation, peer influence and personal preferences also affect final purchase decisions. The study concluded that influencer credibility is a strong but culturally dependent determinant of consumer purchase behaviour. It recommended that influencers maintain authenticity and transparency, and that brands consider cultural alignment when selecting influencers for marketing campaigns.

title: Exploring News Consumption Patterns of Female Digital Natives in Abuja
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Akuta Michelle Idialu, Desmond Onyemechi Okocha, Fidelis Olarinde Olugbamiye
abstract: The emergence of technology has given rise to a shift in the news consumption patterns of media audiences. This study examined the news consumption patterns of Nigeria’s female digital natives, focusing on their preferred media platforms, news interests, attitudes toward traditional and digital sources, and the influence of social media on their news consumption patterns. Guided by Uses and Gratifications and Technological Determinism theories, the study adopted a quantitative survey design, with a sample size of 176. Purposive and snowball sampling techniques were used. Using a structured questionnaire, data were collected from female digital natives in Abuja Municipal Area Council. The findings revealed a strong preference for digital platforms such as Instagram, driven by accessibility, interactivity and real-time updates. The findings also indicated that respondents had greater interest in soft news, such as entertainment and lifestyle, than in hard news, such as politics or business. The study further found that while female digital natives actively select news to satisfy personal needs, their habits are shaped by digital technologies and algorithmic structures. It therefore concluded that the behaviour of female digital natives represents a shift from passive consumption toward interactive, personalised and algorithmically mediated news experiences. The study recommends that traditional and online news outlets increase their presence and engagement on social media platforms where female digital natives are most active in order to enhance their growing interest in news consumption.
